children.title: Convex MIQP
children.top_down_role: MIQP with a convex continuous quadratic relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex MIQP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard minimization-form convex MIQP with linear constraints and a convex continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge1\) and \(m\ge0\), and let \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A convex mixed-integer quadratic program has the form \[\min\left\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in\mathbb R^n,\;Ax\le b,\;x_i\in\mathbb Z\ \text{for every }i\in I\right\},\] where \(Q\succeq0\). Coordinates outside \(I\) are continuous. Removing the integrality restrictions yields a convex quadratic program because the feasible region is polyhedral and the objective has positive-semidefinite Hessian \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex MIQP minimizes a quadratic with a positive-semidefinite Hessian over linear constraints, with designated coordinates integral; removing integrality gives a convex quadratic program.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
\(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The continuous relaxation is a convex quadratic program.

children.title: Indefinite MIQP
children.top_down_role: MIQP requiring global treatment of an indefinite quadratic objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite MIQP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-indefinite MIQP in minimization form; feasible-set restrictions may occasionally remove the nonconvex directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An indefinite mixed-integer quadratic program has the form \[\min\left\{\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P,\;x_i\in\mathbb Z\ (i\in I)\right\},\] where \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a polyhedron, \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), and \(Q\) has both a positive and a negative eigenvalue. Thus the quadratic objective is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb R^n\). Unless the affine hull of \(P\) excludes every negative-curvature direction, the continuous relaxation is a nonconvex quadratic program requiring global rather than purely convex optimization treatment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indefinite MIQP has an objective Hessian with positive and negative eigenvalues; its continuous relaxation is generally nonconvex unless feasibility removes all negative-curvature directions.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral.
\(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\) has eigenvalues of both signs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is indefinite, and the continuous relaxation is nonconvex whenever a feasible negative-curvature direction remains.

children.title: Pure-Integer Quadratic Programming
children.top_down_role: Quadratic optimization with an entirely discrete decision vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Pure-Integer Quadratic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic optimization in which every decision coordinate is integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge1\) and \(m\ge0\), and let \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). A pure-integer quadratic program has the form \[\min\left\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in\mathbb Z^n,\;Ax\le b\right\}.\] Every decision coordinate is integer-valued, so the model has no continuous decision coordinates. The quadratic objective on \(\mathbb R^n\) is convex exactly when \(Q\succeq0\), while the optimization feasible set remains discrete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pure-integer quadratic program optimizes a quadratic function over an entirely integer-valued vector subject to linear constraints; it has no continuous decision coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
\(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible decision vector belongs to \(\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax\le b\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex MIQCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization-form MIQCP whose integrality relaxation is a convex quadratically constrained quadratic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex mixed-integer quadratically constrained program has the form \[\min\{q_0(x):q_r(x)\le0\ (r=1,\ldots,m),\;Ax=b,\;x_i\in\mathbb Z\ (i\in I)\},\] where \(q_r(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_rx+c_r^{\mathsf T}x+d_r\), every \(Q_r\) for \(r=0,\ldots,m\) is positive semidefinite, and all equality constraints are affine. After replacing integrality by real-valued domains, the objective and inequality functions are convex and the feasible region is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex MIQCP has a convex quadratic objective, convex quadratic inequalities, affine equalities, and selected integer variables; dropping integrality produces a convex QCQP.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_r=Q_r^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\) for \(r=0,\ldots,m\).
All equality constraints are affine.
\(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The continuous relaxation is a convex quadratically constrained quadratic program.

notation.meaning: Hessian matrix of the corresponding quadratic function

children.title: Bilinear MIQCP

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear MIQCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: MIQCP containing explicit products of distinct variables in its objective or constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bilinear MIQCP is a mixed-integer quadratically constrained program in which at least one objective or constraint function contains a nonzero term \(\alpha x_jx_k\) with \(j\ne k\). In a symmetric quadratic representation \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx\), this corresponds to nonzero off-diagonal entries satisfying \(Q_{jk}=Q_{kj}\). A pure isolated product \(\alpha x_jx_k\) has an indefinite Hessian when \(\alpha\ne0\); additional diagonal quadratic terms can nevertheless make the complete quadratic function convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear MIQCP contains a product of two distinct variables. Such a product is intrinsically indefinite in isolation, although other quadratic terms may restore overall convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(j\ne k\).
\(\alpha\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model contains a nonzero cross-product term \(\alpha x_jx_k\).

notation.meaning: symmetric matrix representing a quadratic function

children.title: Indefinite MIQCP
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer quadratically constrained models featuring indefinite quadratic forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite MIQCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: MIQCP with indefinite curvature in its objective or a quadratic inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An indefinite MIQCP is a mixed-integer quadratically constrained program for which the symmetric Hessian \(Q_r\) of the quadratic objective or of at least one inequality function has eigenvalues of both signs. Consequently, that function is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb R^n\). If its negative-curvature directions are not eliminated by the affine hull and bounds of the continuous relaxation, the resulting continuous QCQP is nonconvex and local optimality alone does not certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indefinite MIQCP contains an objective or quadratic inequality whose Hessian has eigenvalues of both signs, generally making its continuous relaxation nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: For some index \(r\), \(Q_r=Q_r^{\mathsf T}\) has positive and negative eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The associated quadratic function is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: Hessian matrix of a quadratic objective or inequality

children.title: Bilinear Terms under Indefinite Curvature
children.top_down_role: Regimes where bilinear structure occurs within broader indefinite quadratic geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Terms under Indefinite Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral curvature of an isolated nonzero bilinear cross-product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(s,t)=\alpha st\) with \(\alpha\ne0\), the Hessian is \[\nabla^2f=\begin{pmatrix}0&\alpha\\\alpha&0\end{pmatrix},\] whose eigenvalues are \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\). Hence every nonzero isolated bilinear term has one positive-curvature and one negative-curvature direction and is neither convex nor concave on any open convex subset of \(\mathbb R^2\). In a larger quadratic expression, this conclusion applies to the bilinear component; the inertia of the full Hessian also depends on its diagonal and other cross terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero isolated bilinear product has one positive and one negative Hessian eigenvalue, although the full quadratic expression may have different curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(f(s,t)=\alpha st\) with \(\alpha\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Hessian eigenvalues are \(\alpha\) and \(-\alpha\), so \(f\) is indefinite.

children.title: Quadratic-Equality MIQCP
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer models containing quadratic equality constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Equality MIQCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: MIQCP containing at least one genuinely quadratic equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic-equality MIQCP contains a constraint \[q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d=0\] with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\ne0\), together with integrality restrictions on a designated subset of coordinates. Even when \(Q\succeq0\), the equality is the conjunction of \(q(x)\le0\) and \(-q(x)\le0\); the second inequality is generally nonconvex. Thus a nonaffine quadratic equality is not classified as a convex MIQCP constraint, except in degenerate cases where other restrictions reduce its zero set to a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic-equality MIQCP imposes a nonaffine quadratic equation. Such an equality is generally nonconvex even when its quadratic function is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\ne0\).
Some designated coordinates are integer-constrained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint \(q(x)=0\) is genuinely quadratic and generally does not define a convex feasible set.

children.title: Reverse-Convex MIQCP
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer models containing reverse-convex quadratic constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Reverse-Convex MIQCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic reverse-convex inequality formed by reversing a convex quadratic sublevel constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reverse-convex quadratic constraint has the form \[q(x)\ge0,\qquad q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d,\qquad Q\succeq0,\] equivalently \(-q(x)\le0\). A reverse-convex MIQCP contains at least one such constraint and integrality restrictions on selected coordinates. The excluded set \(\{x:q(x)<0\}\) is convex, whereas its complement \(\{x:q(x)\ge0\}\) is generally nonconvex; affine or one-sided domain restrictions may create degenerate convex cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse-convex MIQCP requires a convex quadratic to be nonnegative, leaving the complement of a convex sublevel region, which is generally nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\).
The model contains the inequality \(q(x)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set \(\{x:q(x)\ge0\}\) is generally nonconvex.

notation.meaning: convex quadratic function whose inequality is reversed

knowledge_statements.title: Intersecting Nonconvex Constraint Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: MIQCP regime produced by simultaneous, genuinely nonconvex quadratic feasible-set restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An intersecting nonconvex-constraint MIQCP has a continuous feasible region \[F=P\cap\bigcap_{r=1}^{m}F_r,\qquad m\ge2,\] where \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral and at least two sets \(F_r\) are defined by quadratic equalities, reverse-convex quadratic inequalities, or indefinite quadratic inequalities and are nonconvex on \(P\). Integrality is imposed on a designated coordinate set. The regime concerns the joint intersection: satisfying or convexifying each constraint separately need not describe the convex hull of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This regime intersects at least two genuinely nonconvex quadratic constraint sets with a polyhedron and mixed-integer restrictions; their joint geometry cannot generally be inferred separately.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral.
\(m\ge2\), and at least two sets \(F_r\) are nonconvex on \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The continuous feasible region is \(F=P\cap\bigcap_{r=1}^{m}F_r\), an intersection governed jointly by multiple nonconvex constraints.

notation.meaning: polyhedral portion of the feasible region

children.title: Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Optimization
children.top_down_role: QUBO and equivalent quadratic pseudo-Boolean problem classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: QUBO in minimization form, equivalently a quadratic pseudo-Boolean optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An unconstrained binary quadratic optimization problem has the form \[\min\left\{x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\gamma:x\in\{0,1\}^n\right\},\] where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\). There are no feasibility constraints beyond binary membership. Because \(x_i^2=x_i\) for every binary coordinate, diagonal quadratic terms may be absorbed into the linear coefficients; hence the formulation is equivalent to minimizing a quadratic pseudo-Boolean function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: QUBO minimizes a quadratic function over binary vectors with no additional constraints; binary idempotence lets diagonal quadratic terms be absorbed into linear terms.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is an unconstrained quadratic pseudo-Boolean optimization problem.

notation.meaning: symmetric matrix of pairwise binary interactions

children.title: Constrained Binary Quadratic Optimization
children.top_down_role: Binary quadratic models retaining explicit feasibility constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Constrained Binary Quadratic Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary quadratic optimization retaining a proper explicit feasibility set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), and \(p\ge0\). Let \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and let each \(h_s:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) for \(s\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\) be affine or quadratic. A constrained binary quadratic optimization problem has the form \[\min\left\{x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\gamma:x\in C\right\},\qquad C=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\le b,\;h_s(x)\le0\ \text{for every }s\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\right\},\] where \(C\subsetneq\{0,1\}^n\). Unlike QUBO, feasibility is not determined solely by binary membership because the retained constraints exclude at least one binary vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constrained binary quadratic optimization minimizes a quadratic over a proper subset of the binary hypercube defined by retained linear or quadratic constraints, unlike unconstrained QUBO.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge1\), \(m,p\ge0\), \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\).
\(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and each \(h_s:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is affine or quadratic.
\(C\subsetneq\{0,1\}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic objective is optimized over the explicitly constrained binary set \(C\).

notation.meaning: proper feasible subset of the binary hypercube
retained affine or quadratic constraint function

children.title: Quadratic Knapsack Models
children.top_down_role: Quadratic interaction objectives over capacity-constrained discrete selections.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Knapsack Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical binary quadratic knapsack formulation with one capacity constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given profits \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}\), interaction coefficients \(q_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\), weights \(a_i\ge 0\), and capacity \(b\ge 0\), a quadratic knapsack model is
\[
\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}q_{ij}x_ix_j:\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\le b\right\}.
\]
The binary variable \(x_i\) indicates selection of item \(i\); the quadratic term assigns a joint reward or penalty to selecting items \(i\) and \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic knapsack model selects capacity-limited binary items while accounting for both individual profits and pairwise interaction rewards or penalties.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\)
\(a\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}_+\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{p^\top x+\sum_{i<j}q_{ij}x_ix_j:a^\top x\le b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\) is a quadratic knapsack problem.

notation.meaning: Binary selection indicator for item i.

children.title: Quadratic Assignment Models
children.top_down_role: Quadratic interaction objectives over assignment or permutation structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Assignment Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Koopmans–Beckmann binary formulation of quadratic assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For facilities and locations indexed by \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(f_{ik}\) be the flow from facility \(i\) to facility \(k\), let \(d_{j\ell}\) be the cost or distance from location \(j\) to location \(\ell\), and let \(c_{ij}\) be a linear assignment cost. The quadratic assignment model is
\[
\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{\ell=1}^n f_{ik}d_{j\ell}x_{ij}x_{k\ell}+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}=1\ \text{for every }i=1,\ldots,n,\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}=1\ \text{for every }j=1,\ldots,n\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic assignment bijectively assigns each facility to one location and each location to one facility while minimizing pairwise flow-distance cost, optionally with linear assignment costs.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\)
\(f,d,c\) are finite real arrays of the displayed dimensions
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is constrained to be a permutation matrix, and the objective evaluates pairwise assignment interactions together with any linear assignment costs.

notation.meaning: One when facility i is assigned to location j.
Flow from facility i to facility k.
Cost or distance from location j to location ell.
Linear cost of assigning facility i to location j.

children.title: Capacity–Permutation Hybrid Structure
children.top_down_role: Quadratic models coupling capacity restrictions with assignment structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity–Permutation Hybrid Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic assignment structure augmented by resource-capacity inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) assign facility \(i\) to location \(j\). A capacity–permutation hybrid has the form
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{i,k,j,\ell}q_{ikj\ell}x_{ij}x_{k\ell}+\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_jx_{ij}=1,\ \sum_ix_{ij}=1,\ \sum_i a_{ri}x_{ij}\le b_{rj}\ \text{for all }r,j\right\}.
\]
Thus its feasible set is the intersection of the permutation-matrix set with capacity knapsack inequalities indexed by resource \(r\) and location \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hybrid combines permutation assignments, local resource capacities, and quadratic interactions among assignment decisions.
assumptions_latex: All index sets are finite.
\(a_{ri}\ge 0\) and \(b_{rj}\ge 0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=\{x\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}:x\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1},\ x^\top\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1},\ \sum_i a_{ri}x_{ij}\le b_{rj}\}\) couples permutation and capacity structure.

children.title: Max-Cut Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Binary quadratic structure viewed through weighted graph partitioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Max-Cut Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion of weighted Max-Cut into a binary quadratic objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with edge weights \(w_{uv}\in\mathbb{R}\). Encode a vertex shore by \(x_v\in\{0,1\}\). Since an edge \(\{u,v\}\) crosses the cut exactly when \(x_u+x_v-2x_ux_v=1\), weighted Max-Cut is represented by
\[
\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{V}}\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}w_{uv}(x_u+x_v-2x_ux_v).
\]
Every binary vector defines a cut, and complementary vectors \(x\) and \(\mathbf{1}-x\) define the same cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted Max-Cut is a binary quadratic optimization problem whose edge term equals one exactly when its endpoints lie on opposite shores.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
\(w_{uv}\in\mathbb{R}\) for every \(\{u,v\}\in E\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{MaxCut}(G,w)=\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{V}}\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}w_{uv}(x_u+x_v-2x_ux_v)\).

notation.meaning: Binary shore label of vertex v.
Weight of edge joining u and v.

knowledge_statements.title: Ising Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine equivalence between QUBO variables and Ising spins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and introduce spins \(s\in\{-1,1\}^n\) by \(x_i=(1+s_i)/2\). For a QUBO objective \(f(x)=x^\top Qx+c^\top x+\kappa\), substitution yields an Ising energy
\[
f((\mathbf{1}+s)/2)=\frac14s^\top Qs+\frac12(Q\mathbf{1}+c)^\top s+\kappa+\frac14\mathbf{1}^\top Q\mathbf{1}+\frac12c^\top\mathbf{1},
\]
provided \(Q\) is symmetric. The bijection preserves feasible assignments and objective ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing each binary variable by an affine spin variable converts any symmetric QUBO into an equivalent Ising energy, up to an additive constant.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric.
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\kappa\in\mathbb{R}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bijection \(s=2x-\mathbf{1}\) gives an objective-equivalent Ising formulation on \(\{-1,1\}^n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine QUBO-to-Ising conversion and displayed coefficients are correct for symmetric Q, but no evidence source is supplied.

children.title: Graphical-Model Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Binary quadratic objectives arising from pairwise graphical-model structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Graphical-Model Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise binary MAP inference represented as unconstrained binary quadratic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), binary labels \(x_v\in\{0,1\}\), unary potentials \(\theta_v\), and pairwise potentials \(\theta_{uv}\), maximum a posteriori inference maximizes
\[
\sum_{v\in V}\theta_v(x_v)+\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}\theta_{uv}(x_u,x_v).
\]
Every binary pairwise potential has a unique multilinear representation \(\alpha_{uv}+\beta_{uv}x_u+\gamma_{uv}x_v+\delta_{uv}x_ux_v\). Consequently, the MAP objective is a QUBO plus an additive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary pairwise graphical-model MAP inference is exactly a QUBO because every unary or pairwise potential has a multilinear binary representation.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
Each variable has domain \(\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\arg\max_x\bigl(\sum_v\theta_v(x_v)+\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}\theta_{uv}(x_u,x_v)\bigr)\) equals the optimizer set of a QUBO.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pairwise binary-potential correspondence with a QUBO is mathematically sound and appropriately classified as a representation, but it has no cited source.

children.title: Representation Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Structural mappings among cut, spin, and pairwise graphical representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of binary quadratic objectives under affine complementation and spin recoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), the identities \(x_i^2=x_i\), \(x_i=(1+s_i)/2\), and \(1-x_i\in\{0,1\}\) imply that diagonal quadratic terms, linear terms, variable complements, and Ising spins all remain within the class of degree-two pseudo-Boolean functions. Hence any objective \(x^\top Qx+c^\top x+\kappa\) can be rewritten, without changing optimizer correspondence, using symmetric QUBO coefficients, complemented binary variables, or pairwise spin interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: QUBO, complemented-binary, and pairwise Ising objectives are algebraically equivalent representations of degree-two pseudo-Boolean functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degree-two pseudo-Boolean objectives are invariant as a representation class under \(x_i\mapsto1-x_i\) and \(x_i\mapsto(1+s_i)/2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closure and representation correspondences are standard and internally consistent, but the record supplies no source for the pseudo-Boolean, complemented-variable, and Ising equivalences.

children.title: Smooth Convex MINLP
children.top_down_role: Convex MINLP with differentiable nonlinear structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex MINLP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable convex MINLP over a mixed-integer convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A smooth convex mixed-integer nonlinear program has the form
\[
\min\{f(x,y):g_j(x,y)\le0\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,m,\ (x,y)\in X,\ x\in\mathbb{Z}^p\},
\]
where \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p+q}\) is convex, and \(f\) and every \(g_j\) are convex and continuously differentiable on an open convex neighborhood of \(X\). Integrality makes the feasible set nonconvex, while the continuous relaxation obtained by replacing \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^p\) with \(x\in\mathbb{R}^p\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex MINLP has integer variables but convex, continuously differentiable objective and constraint functions, yielding a convex continuous relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p+q}\) is convex.
\(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) are convex and continuously differentiable near \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relaxing \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^p\) to \(x\in\mathbb{R}^p\) produces a smooth convex nonlinear program.

children.title: Nonsmooth Convex MINLP
children.top_down_role: Convex mixed-integer nonlinear models with nonsmooth functions or value representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Convex MINLP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex MINLP permitting nondifferentiable objective and constraint functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonsmooth convex mixed-integer nonlinear program is
\[
\min\{f(x,y):g_j(x,y)\le0\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,m,\ (x,y)\in X,\ x\in\mathbb{Z}^p\},
\]
where \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p+q}\) is convex and \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) are proper closed convex functions, with at least one function not required to be differentiable. Its continuous relaxation remains a convex optimization problem, and supporting inequalities may be generated from subgradients at points in the functions' relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth convex MINLP retains convexity of its continuous relaxation but allows proper closed convex objective or constraint functions without derivatives.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p+q}\) is convex.
\(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) are proper closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^p\) by \(x\in\mathbb{R}^p\) yields a possibly nonsmooth convex program.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential when used at z.

children.title: Conic Convex MINLP
children.top_down_role: Convex mixed-integer nonlinear models represented through supported cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Convex MINLP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-integer convex optimization expressed by affine membership in closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A conic convex mixed-integer nonlinear program has the form
\[
\min\{c^\top z:Az-b\in K,\ z_i\in\mathbb{Z}\ \text{for }i\in I\},
\]
where \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_r\) is a product of closed convex cones and all remaining variables are real. Bounds and affine equalities may be represented by additional cone factors. After removing the integrality restrictions, the feasible set is convex because it is the affine preimage of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic convex MINLP imposes integrality on selected variables while expressing the continuous constraints as affine membership in closed convex cones.
assumptions_latex: \(K_1,\ldots,K_r\) are closed convex cones.
\(A,b,c\) have compatible finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:Az-b\in K\}\) is the convex continuous relaxation before any additional affine restrictions.

notation.meaning: Combined integer and continuous variable vector.

source_refs.locator: Subgradient based outer approximation for mixed integer second order cone programming p. 41

source_witnesses.locator: Subgradient based outer approximation for mixed integer second order cone programming p. 41

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The general conic mixed-integer formulation is mathematically plausible, but the cited locator concerns mixed-integer second-order cone programming and does not adequately support the asserted extension to arbitrary products of closed convex cones.

children.title: Epigraphical Nonsmooth Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Epigraph-based interfaces for structured nonsmooth convex expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Nonsmooth Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph reformulation of convex nonsmooth objectives and constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper closed convex. Minimizing \(f(z)\) over a mixed-integer set \(S\) is equivalently represented as
\[
\min\{t:(z,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f,\ z\in S\},\qquad \operatorname{epi}f=\{(z,t):f(z)\le t\}.
\]
If \(f(z)=\max_{k=1,\ldots,r}f_k(z)\), then epigraph membership is exactly the finite system \(f_k(z)\le t\) for every \(k\), preserving the integer restrictions in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epigraph variable replaces a nonsmooth convex objective by minimizing a scalar subject to convex upper-bound constraints, without altering the integer restrictions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and may impose integrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{z\in S}f(z)=\inf\{t:(z,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f,\ z\in S\}\).

source_refs.locator: Algorithms and software for convex mixed integer nonlinear programs p. 1

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Second-Order Cone Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-integer linear optimization constrained by Lorentz-cone memberships.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A mixed-integer second-order cone program has a linear objective, selected integer variables, affine equations, and constraints
\[
\lVert A_k z+a_k\rVert_2\le b_k^\top z+\beta_k,\qquad k=1,\ldots,r.
\]
Equivalently, \((b_k^\top z+\beta_k,A_kz+a_k)\) belongs to the Lorentz cone \(\mathcal{Q}^{m_k+1}=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{m_k}:\lVert u\rVert_2\le t\}\). Relaxing the selected integrality restrictions therefore yields a second-order cone program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A MISOCP combines integer restrictions with linear constraints and norm inequalities representable by Lorentz-cone membership.
assumptions_latex: All problem data have compatible finite dimensions.
A specified subset of components of \(z\) is integer-constrained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each inequality \(\lVert A_kz+a_k\rVert_2\le b_k^\top z+\beta_k\) is equivalent to membership in \(\mathcal{Q}^{m_k+1}\).

notation.meaning: Combined integer and continuous decision vector.

children.title: Mixed-Integer Semidefinite Models
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer models containing positive-semidefinite matrix constraints.

assumptions_latex: The data matrices satisfy \(F_i\in\mathbb S^m\) for \(i=0,\ldots,n\).
The integer index set satisfies \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible region is \(\{x\in\mathbb R^n:F_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iF_i\succeq0,\ Ax=b,\ x_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\}\).

notation.meaning: Space of real symmetric matrices of order m

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses an affine matrix inequality with selected scalar variables constrained to be integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A mixed-integer semidefinite model optimizes a linear objective \(c^\top x\) over real variables \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), with \(x_i\in\mathbb Z\) for every \(i\in I\), subject to affine equalities and an affine positive-semidefinite constraint. Its canonical form is
\[\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ F_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iF_i\succeq0,\ x_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\}.\]
Additional affine inequalities may be represented using nonnegative slack variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-integer semidefinite model combines linear objectives and constraints, integrality restrictions, and an affine positive-semidefinite matrix constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Semidefinite Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the semidefinite-model leaf, but no source is cited. A source must support the mixed-integer semidefinite canonical form and supply a specific locator. The domains or dimensions of c, A, and b should also be stated before promotion.

children.title: Mixed-Integer Exponential-Cone Models
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer models represented with exponential-cone structure.

assumptions_latex: The exponential-cone arguments are real affine functions of the decision vector.
The integer index set satisfies \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonlinear constraint has the form \((a_j^\top x+\alpha_j,b_j^\top x+\beta_j,d_j^\top x+\delta_j)\in K_{\exp}\), together with \(x_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the closed primal exponential cone and affine conic inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the closed exponential cone by
\[K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\leq w\}.\]
A mixed-integer exponential-cone model optimizes a linear function of \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), imposes \(x_i\in\mathbb Z\) for \(i\in I\), and requires finitely many affine images of \(x\) to belong to \(K_{\exp}\), possibly alongside affine equalities and other conic constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This model combines integer variables with affine inclusions in the closed exponential cone, thereby representing exponential, logarithmic, entropy, and relative-entropy relations.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Exponential-Cone Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the exponential-cone leaf and the closed-cone formula is standard, but no source is cited. The conclusion says every nonlinear constraint is an exponential-cone inclusion, whereas the statement permits other conic constraints; the intended scope must be resolved against an authoritative source.

children.title: Mixed-Integer Power-Cone Models
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer models represented with power-cone structure.

assumptions_latex: A cone parameter satisfies \(0<\alpha<1\).
The integer index set satisfies \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every power-cone constraint is an affine inclusion in \(K_\alpha\), while \(x_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\).

notation.meaning: Three-dimensional power cone with exponent alpha

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard three-dimensional primal power cone with fixed exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define the power cone
\[K_\alpha=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:u\geq0,\ v\geq0,\ u^\alpha v^{1-\alpha}\geq|w|\}.\]
A mixed-integer power-cone model optimizes a linear function of \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), imposes \(x_i\in\mathbb Z\) for every \(i\in I\), and constrains finitely many affine images of \(x\) to lie in power cones, possibly with different fixed exponents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-integer power-cone model combines integrality restrictions with affine inclusions in fixed-exponent power cones.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Power-Cone Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-exponent power-cone definition is mathematically standard and the definition kind fits this leaf, but the record has no inspectable source supporting the cone convention and mixed-integer model class.

children.title: Other Mixed-Integer Extended-Cone Models
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer conic regimes beyond second-order, semidefinite, exponential, or power cones.

assumptions_latex: Each \(K_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{m_j}\) is a specified closed convex cone.
The index set \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) identifies integer variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model class is \(\min\{c^\top x:A_jx+b_j\in K_j\ (j=1,\ldots,q),\ x_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\}\).

notation.meaning: A closed convex cone from the selected extended-cone library

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers closed convex cones beyond the semidefinite, exponential, and power-cone subclasses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_1,\ldots,K_q\) be specified closed convex cones, including at least one cone outside the semidefinite, exponential, and power-cone families. An other mixed-integer extended-cone model has linear objective, affine conic inclusions \(A_jx+b_j\in K_j\), and integrality restrictions \(x_i\in\mathbb Z\) for \(i\in I\). The designation is relative to the adopted cone library; it does not assert that the cones lack representations using larger products or lifts of named cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This residual class consists of mixed-integer conic models using specified closed convex cones outside the three named extended-cone families.
knowledge_statements.title: Other Mixed-Integer Extended-Cone Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for this residual model-family leaf, but the adopted cone library and the meaning of exclusion from the three named families are source-dependent and currently unsupported. A specific source and locator are required.

children.title: Structured Factorable MINLP Family

children.title: Factorable Nonconvex MINLP
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex mixed-integer models exposed through compositions of elementary operators.

assumptions_latex: The variable domain satisfies \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
The integer index set satisfies \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
A finite primitive library \(\mathcal L\) of unary and binary operations is fixed, and every primitive is evaluated only on its declared domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonlinear objective or constraint function admits a finite directed acyclic evaluation graph whose leaves are variables or constants and whose internal nodes apply members of \(\mathcal L\).

notation.meaning: Fixed library of admissible elementary operations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorability is relative to a declared finite library of elementary operations and their domains.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 The structured nonconvex mixed integer nonlinear program p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and fix a finite primitive library \(\mathcal L\). A factorable nonconvex MINLP is a problem
\[\min\{f_0(x):f_r(x)\leq0\ \text{for }r=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in X,\ x_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\},\]
where each function \(f_r:X\to\mathbb R\), for \(r=0,\ldots,m\), is represented by a finite directed acyclic graph. Every leaf is a component of \(x\) or a constant, and every internal node applies an operation from \(\mathcal L\) on its declared domain. Convexity is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factorable nonconvex MINLP represents every nonlinear objective and constraint by a finite computation graph of declared elementary operations, while requiring selected variables to be integral.
knowledge_statements.title: Factorable Nonconvex MINLP

children.title: Separable Nonconvex MINLP
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex mixed-integer models decomposed into variable-disjoint or weakly coupled terms.

assumptions_latex: The variable vector satisfies \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
The integer index set satisfies \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
Each component function is defined on the projection of \(X\) onto its argument coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every objective or constraint function satisfies \(f_r(x)=\beta_r+\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{ri}(x_i)\), where each \(\phi_{ri}\) is univariate.

notation.meaning: Univariate component of function r associated with coordinate i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses additive coordinate separability; component functions may be nonconvex.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Separable reformulation of factorable programs p. 15
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A separable nonconvex MINLP is a problem
\[\min\{f_0(x):f_r(x)\leq0\ \text{for }r=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in X,\ x_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\},\]
in which every objective or constraint function has the representation
\[f_r(x)=\beta_r+\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_{ri}(x_i),\qquad r=0,\ldots,m,\]
for univariate functions \(\phi_{ri}\). The component functions need not be convex. Affine terms are included by choosing affine components, and absent coordinates are represented by zero components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable nonconvex MINLP expresses every objective and constraint as an additive sum of univariate coordinate functions, which may be nonconvex, and restricts selected coordinates to integer values.
knowledge_statements.title: Separable Nonconvex MINLP

children.top_down_role: Factorable nonlinear models whose expression structure also supports blockwise separation.

assumptions_latex: The variable vector satisfies \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
The coordinate sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_q\) form a partition of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
The integer index set satisfies \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
Every block function is factorable over a fixed primitive library \(\mathcal L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(r=0,\ldots,m\), the function satisfies \(f_r(x)=\beta_r+\sum_{k=1}^q f_{rk}(x_{B_k})\), with every \(f_{rk}\) factorable over \(\mathcal L\).

notation.meaning: Factorable contribution of block k to function r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines additive block separability with factorability inside each disjoint variable block.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), fix a primitive library \(\mathcal L\), and let \(B_1,\ldots,B_q\) partition \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A factorable block-separable MINLP is a problem
\[\min\{f_0(x):f_r(x)\leq0\ \text{for }r=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in X,\ x_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\},\]
in which, for every \(r=0,\ldots,m\),
\[f_r(x)=\beta_r+\sum_{k=1}^q f_{rk}(x_{B_k}),\]
and each block function \(f_{rk}\) is factorable over \(\mathcal L\). Linear coupling constraints may involve several blocks without altering the stated block separability of the nonlinear functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factorable block-separable MINLP expresses every nonlinear objective and constraint as a sum of factorable functions on disjoint variable blocks, while allowing linear constraints to couple blocks.

children.title: Polynomial MINLP
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer nonlinear models built from polynomial expressions.

assumptions_latex: Every polynomial has finitely many terms with nonnegative integer exponent vectors.
The variable domain satisfies \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each objective or constraint function is \(p_r(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in A_r}c_{r\alpha}x^\alpha\), where \(A_r\subset\mathbb N^n\) is finite.

notation.meaning: Finite exponent set for polynomial r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial exponents are nonnegative integers; coefficients and variables are real.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A polynomial MINLP is a problem
\[\min\{p_0(x):p_r(x)\leq0\ (r=1,\ldots,m),\ x\in X,\ x_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\},\]
where every \(p_r\) is a real multivariate polynomial
\[p_r(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in A_r}c_{r\alpha}x^\alpha,\qquad x^\alpha=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha_i},\]
and each \(A_r\) is a finite subset of \(\mathbb N^n\). Neither the polynomials nor the continuous relaxation are required to be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial MINLP has polynomial objectives and constraints with nonnegative integer exponents, plus integrality restrictions on selected variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial MINLP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polynomial formula and definition kind fit the leaf, but no source is provided. The record also uses I without explicitly declaring its subset relation. A polynomial-MINLP source with a specific locator is required before the mathematical version can be settled.

children.title: Signomial MINLP
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer nonlinear models containing signomial expressions.

assumptions_latex: The variable vector satisfies \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
The integer index set satisfies \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
Each signomial contains finitely many terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each nonlinear function is \(s_r(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{q_r}c_{rk}\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_{rki}}\), where \(q_r\in\mathbb N\), \(c_{rk}\in\mathbb R\), and \(a_{rki}\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Real exponent of variable i in term k of function r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses finite real-exponent signomials on the strictly positive orthant.

source_refs.locator: Global optimization of mixed-integer signomial programming problems p. 349

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A signomial MINLP is an optimization problem over \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), with \(x_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\), in which every nonlinear objective or constraint function has the form
\[s_r(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{q_r}c_{rk}\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_{rki}},\]
where \(q_r\in\mathbb N\), \(c_{rk}\in\mathbb R\), and \(a_{rki}\in\mathbb R\). Negative coefficients and arbitrary real exponents are permitted, so the functions need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A signomial MINLP uses finite sums of real-coefficient monomials with arbitrary real exponents over strictly positive variables, together with explicitly selected integer restrictions.
knowledge_statements.title: Signomial MINLP

children.title: Algebraic Representation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representability limits separating polynomial, signomial, and more general factorable structure.

assumptions_latex: An extended polynomial formulation uses finitely many auxiliary real variables and polynomial equalities and inequalities.
Exact representation means equality after projection onto the original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A set that is not semialgebraic cannot have an exact finite polynomial extended formulation; in particular, the graph \(\{(x,y):x\in(a,b),\ y=\exp(x)\}\) has none.

notation.meaning: A finite system of polynomial equalities and inequalities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks the exact finite polynomial-lifting boundary, not approximation by polynomial constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) is described by finitely many polynomial equalities and inequalities, then its projection \(\pi_x(S)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is semialgebraic. Consequently, any feasible set that is not semialgebraic cannot be represented exactly by a finite polynomial lifting. For every nonempty open interval \((a,b)\), the graph
\[G=\{(x,y)\in(a,b)\times\mathbb R:y=\exp(x)\}\]
is not semialgebraic and therefore admits no exact finite extended formulation consisting solely of polynomial equalities and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite polynomial liftings represent only semialgebraic sets; transcendental graphs such as the exponential graph on an open interval lie beyond this exact representation class.
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Representation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is appropriate, and the projection implication is mathematically plausible, but the record cites no source for either Tarski-Seidenberg or the nonsemialgebraicity of the exponential graph on an arbitrary nonempty open interval. children.title: Deterministic Convexification Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on deterministic relaxation construction caused by missing expression structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Convexification Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary for deterministic convexification of explicit nonconvex MINLP expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) contain a nonempty interval, and let an algorithm obtain an unknown function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) only through finitely many value queries. Two functions can agree at every queried point while having different convex envelopes on \(D\). Consequently, finite deterministic querying cannot identify \(\operatorname{conv} f\) for every admissible \(f\). Guaranteed expression-based convexification therefore requires additional structure, such as a known factorization, recognized primitive functions, valid variable bounds, or derivative information; outside that interface, the constructed relaxation need not be the convex envelope or even a valid global underestimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite black-box evaluations cannot determine every function's convex envelope. Deterministic convexification needs explicit structural information such as factorization, recognized primitives, bounds, or derivatives.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) contains a nonempty interval.
The admissible function class is not restricted by a known finite-dimensional representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite value-oracle information alone does not determine \(\operatorname{conv} f\) on \(D\).

notation.meaning: convex envelope of the function over its stated domain
bounded or otherwise specified continuous domain

review_flags: scope relative to derivative oracles requires review

children.title: Constraint-Penalty Encodings
children.top_down_role: Encodings that absorb selected discrete restrictions into a quadratic objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Penalty Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact quadratic penalties for equality-constrained binary optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(v^*=\min\{c(x):x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ g_k(x)=0\ (k=1,\ldots,m)\}\), where every \(g_k\) is integer-valued on the binary cube and the feasible set is nonempty. Define \(Q_\rho(x)=c(x)+\sum_{k=1}^m\rho_k g_k(x)^2\), and let \(\Delta=\max_x c(x)-\min_x c(x)\), with both extrema over \(\{0,1\}^n\). If \(\rho_k>\Delta\) for every \(k\), then every global minimizer of \(Q_\rho\) is feasible and attains \(v^*\). When \(c\) and all \(g_k^2\) are quadratic pseudo-Boolean functions, \(Q_\rho\) is a QUBO encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer-valued equality violations can be squared and penalized. Penalties exceeding the objective range make every global QUBO minimizer feasible and optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(c:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is bounded.
\(g_k:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{Z}\) for every \(k\).
The equality-constrained feasible set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\min_k\rho_k>\Delta\), then \(\arg\min Q_\rho\subseteq\arg\min\{c(x):g(x)=0\}\).

notation.meaning: range of the original objective on the binary cube

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Lagrangian Relaxation and Dual Formulation p. 45

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1 Lagrangian Relaxation and Dual Formulation p. 45

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically coherent and fits constraint-penalty encodings, but the cited Lagrangian-relaxation locator does not specifically support the stated finite exact squared-penalty threshold. children.title: Explicit-Constraint Recovery
children.top_down_role: Reformulations that restore explicit constraints or auxiliary decisions from QUBO form.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Constraint Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of constrained binary models from exact QUBO penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a QUBO has the decomposition \(Q(x,s)=f(x,s)+P(x,s)\) on \(\{0,1\}^{n+r}\), where \(P(x,s)\geq0\) and \(P(x,s)=0\) exactly when \((x,s)\in F\). Restoring the explicit constraint \((x,s)\in F\) and deleting \(P\) gives \(\min\{f(x,s):(x,s)\in F\}\). If the penalty is exact, meaning every minimizer of \(Q\) belongs to \(F\), then the two formulations have the same optimal value and the same optimal pairs. Projection onto \(x\) recovers the original decisions; auxiliary decisions are recovered from \(S(x)=\{s:(x,s)\in F\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact QUBO penalty can be removed while its zero set is restored as explicit constraints; projection then recovers original decisions and feasible auxiliaries.
assumptions_latex: \(P(x,s)=0\) if and only if \((x,s)\in F\).
Every global minimizer of \(Q\) lies in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\arg\min Q=\arg\min\{f(x,s):(x,s)\in F\}\).

notation.meaning: explicit feasible set encoded by zero penalty
auxiliary completions feasible for an original decision

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Lagrangian Relaxation and Dual Formulation p. 45

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1 Lagrangian Relaxation and Dual Formulation p. 45

children.title: Fortet Hulls

knowledge_statements.title: Fortet Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideal linear formulation of one binary product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary variables \(x,y\) and a product variable \(w\), the Fortet polytope is \[F=\{(x,y,w)\in[0,1]^3:w\leq x,\ w\leq y,\ w\geq x+y-1,\ w\geq0\}.\] It is an ideal formulation: \[F=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,w)\in\{0,1\}^3:w=xy\}.\] Hence every vertex of \(F\) is binary, and imposing binary restrictions on \(x\) and \(y\) forces \(w=xy\) without requiring \(w\) itself to be declared binary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four Fortet inequalities describe exactly the convex hull of a binary product, and binary factors force the auxiliary variable to equal their product.
assumptions_latex: \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\) in the discrete product set.
\(w\) represents \(xy\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed polytope equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,xy):x,y\in\{0,1\}\}\).

notation.meaning: auxiliary variable representing the binary product

children.title: Binary McCormick Hulls

knowledge_statements.title: Binary McCormick Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: McCormick envelope specialized to two binary factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \((x,y)\in[0,1]^2\), the McCormick relaxation of \(w=xy\) is \[M=\{(x,y,w):w\geq0,\ w\geq x+y-1,\ w\leq x,\ w\leq y\}.\] These four inequalities are the convex and concave envelope inequalities for the bilinear graph over the unit box. When \(x\) and \(y\) are binary, \(M\) is ideal and equals the convex hull of the four graph points \((0,0,0)\), \((0,1,0)\), \((1,0,0)\), and \((1,1,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit-box McCormick inequalities form an ideal hull for a product of two binary variables.
assumptions_latex: The intended graph equation is \(w=xy\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,xy):x,y\in\{0,1\}\}\).

children.title: Binary Product Hull Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural equivalence between canonical hull descriptions for binary products.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Product Hull Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of Fortet and unit-box McCormick product formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=\{(x,y,w)\in\{0,1\}^2\times\mathbb{R}:w=xy\}\). The Fortet formulation and the McCormick formulation obtained from the bounds \(0\leq x,y\leq1\) both define \[\operatorname{conv}(G)=\{(x,y,w)\in[0,1]^3:w\geq0,\ w\geq x+y-1,\ w\leq x,\ w\leq y\}.\] Thus the two names describe the same three-dimensional binary-product hull. In particular, either formulation is ideal, and its projection onto the factor variables is the entire unit square.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fortet linearization and the unit-box McCormick formulation are the same ideal convex hull for one binary product.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(y\) are binary in the underlying graph.
Their continuous relaxation uses the exact bounds \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Fortet and binary McCormick polytopes both equal \(\operatorname{conv}(G)\).

children.title: Binary Linearization Size-Strength Tradeoff

children.title: Compact Linearizations
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary-variable linearizations designed to limit formulation size.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Linearizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termwise linearization using one auxiliary per retained binary product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\subseteq\{\{i,j\}:1\leq i<j\leq n\}\) index the products occurring in a quadratic binary model. Introduce one continuous variable \(w_{ij}\) for each \(\{i,j\}\in E\) and impose \[0\leq w_{ij},\qquad w_{ij}\leq x_i,\qquad w_{ij}\leq x_j,\qquad w_{ij}\geq x_i+x_j-1.\] Replacing every occurrence of \(x_ix_j\) by \(w_{ij}\) yields an exact mixed-integer linear representation when \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). The formulation adds \(|E|\) variables and at most \(4|E|\) explicit inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One auxiliary and four hull inequalities per present binary product give an exact linearization whose size is linear in the number of products.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) contains every distinct product replaced in the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The linearized mixed-integer formulation projects exactly onto the original quadratic binary feasible set and objective graph.

notation.meaning: index set of distinct quadratic products
continuous auxiliary for the product of variables indexed by an edge

children.title: Aggregated Linearizations
children.top_down_role: Linearizations that combine multiple binary-product relations into aggregated constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregated Linearizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and relaxation loss under nonnegative aggregation of linearization rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{u\in B:a_r^{\mathsf T}u\leq b_r,\ r=1,\ldots,R\}\) be a disaggregated binary-product relaxation over a base set \(B\). For any weights \(\lambda_r\geq0\), every point of \(P\) satisfies \[\left(\sum_{r=1}^R\lambda_r a_r\right)^{\mathsf T}u\leq\sum_{r=1}^R\lambda_r b_r.\] Hence replacing the selected rows by this aggregate produces a valid relaxation \(P_{\lambda}\) with \(P\subseteq P_{\lambda}\). The aggregation is equivalent only if the deleted rows are implied by the aggregate together with the retained constraints; otherwise it can admit additional fractional points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative row aggregation preserves validity and reduces constraint count, but it weakens the relaxation unless retained constraints recover every deleted inequality.
assumptions_latex: The original rows \(a_r^{\mathsf T}u\leq b_r\) are valid.
Aggregation weights satisfy \(\lambda_r\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\subseteq P_{\lambda}\), with equality exactly when all removed rows remain implied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the terminal container, and the validity and set-inclusion statements are internally correct for the defined row-replacement operation. No citation is supplied for aggregated binary linearizations or their relaxation-strength implications.

children.title: Linearization Size–Strength Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural tradeoffs between compactness and relaxation strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Linearization Size–Strength Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-inclusion ordering of full, aggregated, and omitted product relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed bounded quadratic binary formulation, let \(P_{\mathrm{full}}\) retain every termwise product-hull inequality, let \(P_{\mathrm{agg}}\) replace some groups by valid nonnegative aggregates, and let \(P_{\mathrm{omit}}\) omit those groups while retaining only base bounds. Then \[P_{\mathrm{full}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{agg}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{omit}}.\] For minimization, the associated relaxation bounds satisfy \[z_{\mathrm{omit}}\leq z_{\mathrm{agg}}\leq z_{\mathrm{full}}\leq z_{\mathrm{IP}}.\] Thus fewer rows generally trade formulation size for weaker bounds; equality at either inclusion requires the deleted inequalities to be implied by those retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full product hulls dominate aggregated relaxations, which dominate omitted-row relaxations; minimization lower bounds follow the reverse strength ordering.
assumptions_latex: All three formulations use the same variables, objective, and base bounds.
Aggregated inequalities are nonnegative combinations of full-formulation rows.
The integer formulation is feasible and has finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed feasible-set inclusions and minimization-bound ordering hold.

notation.meaning: integer optimum for a minimization problem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle role fits the size-strength regime leaf, and the feasible-set and minimization-bound orderings are consistent under the stated common-variable assumptions. The record has no source for this binary-linearization taxonomy and its implication conditions.

children.title: Higher-Order Quadratization
children.top_down_role: Reduction of higher-degree pseudo-Boolean structure to quadratic form.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Quadratization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of a pseudo-Boolean function to quadratic degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). A quadratization of \(f\) is a quadratic pseudo-Boolean function \(q:\{0,1\}^{n+r}\to\mathbb{R}\), with auxiliary variables \(y\in\{0,1\}^r\), such that \[f(x)=\min_{y\in\{0,1\}^r}q(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\{0,1\}^n.\] Consequently, \(\min_x f(x)=\min_{x,y}q(x,y)\), and any minimizer \((x^*,y^*)\) of \(q\) projects to a minimizer \(x^*\) of \(f\). The quadratization size is commonly measured by the auxiliary count \(r\) and the number of quadratic terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratization represents every value of a higher-degree pseudo-Boolean function as the minimum of a quadratic function over binary auxiliaries.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a real-valued function on \(\{0,1\}^n\).
Auxiliary variables are binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact pointwise minimization over auxiliaries preserves the global optimum and its projected minimizers.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is the standard pointwise-minimization notion of pseudo-Boolean quadratization and fits the exact leaf. No source is provided for the definition or the stated size measures, so it cannot pass evidence review.

children.title: Roof-Dual Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Relaxation family associated with quadratic pseudo-Boolean optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Roof-Dual Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear roof-dual bound for unconstrained quadratic pseudo-Boolean minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=c+\sum_i a_ix_i+\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}b_{ij}x_ix_j\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Its roof-dual relaxation is the linear program obtained by minimizing \(c+\sum_i a_ix_i+\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}b_{ij}w_{ij}\) subject to \[0\leq x_i\leq1,\qquad \max\{0,x_i+x_j-1\}\leq w_{ij}\leq\min\{x_i,x_j\}.\] Its value is a lower bound on \(\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}f(x)\). An optimal solution may be chosen half-integral in the original variables, meaning \(x_i\in\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The roof-dual LP replaces each binary product by its unit-box hull, yields a lower bound, and admits a half-integral optimal labeling.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is an unconstrained quadratic pseudo-Boolean function.
Every product variable uses the unit-box product inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxation value does not exceed the binary optimum, and a half-integral optimal \(x\) exists.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality kind fits the roof-dual leaf, but the identification of roof duality with the displayed product-variable LP and the half-integral optimal-labeling assertion require a specific authoritative source. Those specialized claims cannot be validated from the supplied inventory alone.

children.title: Persistency-Based Variable-Fixing Certificates

children.title: Persistency Certificates
children.top_down_role: Partial-assignment certificates supported by binary quadratic relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Persistency Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak persistency from integral coordinates of an optimal roof-dual labeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be quadratic, and let \(\bar x\in\{0,\tfrac12,1\}^n\) be an optimal roof-dual labeling. Define \(I=\{i:\bar x_i\in\{0,1\}\}\). The pair \((I,\bar x_I)\) is a weak-persistency certificate: there exists a global binary minimizer \(x^*\) of \(f\) satisfying \(x_i^*=\bar x_i\) for every \(i\in I\). Thus the certified variables may be fixed simultaneously without removing all global optima. Coordinates labeled \(\tfrac12\) receive no fixing certificate from this statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every integral coordinate of an optimal roof-dual labeling can be fixed consistently with at least one global binary optimum; half-integral coordinates remain uncertified.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a quadratic pseudo-Boolean minimization objective.
\(\bar x\) is an optimal labeling of the corresponding roof-dual relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(x^*\in\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}f(x)\) with \(x_I^*=\bar x_I\).

notation.meaning: indices integrally labeled by the roof-dual solution
global binary minimizer consistent with certified labels

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind is correct for this leaf, and the statement is explicitly framed as simultaneous weak persistency rather than strong persistency. A specific roof-dual persistency theorem locator is required to validate that every integral coordinate of the chosen optimal labeling has the asserted common optimal completion.

children.title: Relaxation-Based Variable Fixing

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Based Variable Fixing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incumbent-relative fixing by conditional relaxation bounds; equality does not certify fixing in every optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f^*=\min\{f(x):x\in F\}\), and suppose a feasible incumbent has value \(U\). Let \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\), \(v\in\{0,1\}\), and \(L_i^{1-v}\le\min\{f(x):x\in F,\ x_i=1-v\}\). If \(L_i^{1-v}>U\), then every global minimizer satisfies \(x_i=v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a valid lower bound obtained after imposing the opposite binary value exceeds a feasible incumbent value, every global optimum has the certified binary value.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem with feasible set \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and binary variable \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\).
A feasible incumbent has objective value \(U\), and \(L_i^{1-v}\) is a valid lower bound after imposing \(x_i=1-v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(L_i^{1-v}>U\), then every global minimizer satisfies \(x_i=v\).

notation.meaning: objective value of a feasible incumbent
valid conditional lower bound with the opposite binary value

children.title: Certificate Strength Regimes
children.top_down_role: Weak, strong, and partial persistency regimes governing fixing scope.

assumptions_latex: The original binary optimization problem has at least one global minimizer.
A certificate specifies assignments \(x_i=v_i\) for indices \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong persistency implies weak persistency, but weak persistency need not imply strong persistency.

notation.meaning: set of variables covered by the certificate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard distinction between weak and strong persistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes existential and universal agreement of optimal solutions with certified binary assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X^*\neq\varnothing\) be the set of global minimizers and let a variable-fixing certificate prescribe \(x_i=v_i\) for every \(i\in I\). The certificate is weakly persistent when there exists \(x^*\in X^*\) satisfying \(x_i^*=v_i\) for all \(i\in I\). It is strongly persistent when every \(x^*\in X^*\) satisfies those assignments. Strong persistency therefore implies weak persistency. The converse can fail whenever two global minimizers disagree on a certified coordinate, because existential agreement then does not establish universal agreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak persistency preserves at least one optimum; strong persistency fixes the stated values in every optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Strength Regimes

children.title: Submodular Graph-Cut Representation
children.top_down_role: Graph-representable tractable structure in binary quadratic optimization.

assumptions_latex: The energy is a quadratic pseudo-Boolean function on \(\{0,1\}^n\).
Every pairwise coefficient satisfies \(b_{ij}\le 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The energy equals an \(s\)-\(t\) cut capacity plus a constant and is minimized by a minimum cut.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise binary submodularity under the \(0\)-\(1\) multilinear coefficient convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(E(x)=c+\sum_i a_i x_i+\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}x_ix_j\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), pairwise submodularity is equivalent to \(b_{ij}\le0\) for every pair. The identity \(b_{ij}x_ix_j=\frac{b_{ij}}{2}(x_i+x_j)-\frac{b_{ij}}{2}|x_i-x_j|\) expresses each pairwise term as adjusted unary terms plus a cut edge of nonnegative capacity \(-b_{ij}/2\). After representing positive and negative unary coefficients by terminal arcs and an additive constant, there is a capacitated \(s\)-\(t\) graph whose cut capacity equals \(E(x)\) plus a constant. Thus a minimum cut yields a global minimizer of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary quadratic energy with nonpositive pairwise coefficients is exactly representable, up to a constant, as an s-t cut problem.

children.title: Second-Order Cone Representations

assumptions_latex: The matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{S}_+^n\) admits a factorization \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\).
The variables satisfy \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx\le t\) is equivalent to one standard second-order cone constraint.

notation.meaning: factor satisfying Q equals R transpose R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard Lorentz-cone representation of a positive-semidefinite quadratic epigraph.

source_refs.locator: Part VI. Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb{S}_+^n\) and choose \(R\) with \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\). Then the convex quadratic epigraph constraint \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx\le t\) is equivalent to \[\left\|\begin{pmatrix}2Rx\\ t-1\end{pmatrix}\right\|_2\le t+1.\] Indeed, squaring the cone inequality gives \(4\|Rx\|_2^2+(t-1)^2\le(t+1)^2\), which is equivalent to \(\|Rx\|_2^2\,\le t\); the cone inequality also enforces \(t+1\ge0\). Thus a positive-semidefinite quadratic epigraph has an exact standard second-order cone representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factoring a positive-semidefinite quadratic converts its epigraph inequality exactly into a standard Lorentz-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Cone Representations

source_witnesses.locator: Part VI. Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Optimization

children.title: Rotated-Cone Representations

assumptions_latex: The matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{S}_+^n\) has factorization \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\).
The scalar variables satisfy \(u\ge0\) and \(v\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx\le uv\) is equivalent to membership in a rotated second-order cone.

notation.meaning: factor satisfying Q equals R transpose R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rotated-cone encoding of a scaled positive-semidefinite quadratic inequality.

source_refs.locator: Part VI. Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the rotated second-order cone by \(\mathcal Q_r^{m+2}=\{(u,v,w):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\}\). If \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\succeq0\), then \[x^{\mathsf T}Qx\le uv\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (u,v,\sqrt{2}Rx)\in\mathcal Q_r^{m+2}.\] The equivalence follows because the cone inequality becomes \(2uv\ge2\|Rx\|_2^2\). This representation retains both nonnegativity requirements on the scaling variables and remains valid when either scalar is zero, in which case it forces \(Rx=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite quadratic bounded by a product of nonnegative scalars is exactly a rotated-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Rotated-Cone Representations

source_witnesses.locator: Part VI. Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Optimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rotated-cone scaling is correct, but \(m\) is not introduced as the row dimension of \(R\), the citation locator is too broad, and the statement contains derivational text.

children.title: Perspective–Conic Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between perspective structure and rotated-cone representability.

assumptions_latex: The quadratic function is \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx\) with \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\succeq0\).
The activation variable satisfies \(z\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed perspective epigraph is exactly \((t,z,\sqrt{2}Rx)\in\mathcal Q_r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed perspective of a homogeneous positive-semidefinite quadratic, including the zero-activation boundary.

source_refs.locator: Part VI. Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx=\|Rx\|_2^2\), the perspective for \(z>0\) is \(zq(x/z)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx/z\). Its closed epigraph is \[\operatorname{cl}\{(x,z,t):z>0,\ t\ge x^{\mathsf T}Qx/z\}=\{(x,z,t):(t,z,\sqrt{2}Rx)\in\mathcal Q_r\}.\] Consequently, for \(z>0\) the cone condition is equivalent to \(tz\ge x^{\mathsf T}Qx\) with \(t,z\ge0\). At \(z=0\), closure requires \(Rx=0\) and \(t\ge0\); when \(Q\succ0\), this specializes to \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective epigraph of a positive-semidefinite quadratic is exactly representable by a rotated second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Perspective–Conic Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: Part VI. Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Introduce \(X=xx^{\mathsf T}\). Then every quadratic expression satisfies \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2q^{\mathsf T}x+r=\langle Q,X\rangle+2q^{\mathsf T}x+r\). The identity \(X=xx^{\mathsf T}\) is equivalently represented by \[Y=\begin{pmatrix}1&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,\qquad \operatorname{rank}(Y)=1.\] Hence quadratic objectives and constraints become affine in the lifted matrix entries while exactness is carried by the rank condition. Dropping \(\operatorname{rank}(Y)=1\) leaves \(Y\succeq0\), producing a convex semidefinite relaxation that contains every exactly lifted feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lifting X = xx transpose linearizes quadratics; a rank-one positive-semidefinite matrix is exact, while dropping rank gives an SDP relaxation.

children.title: Quadratic Curvature Detection

assumptions_latex: The quadratic function is \(f(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2q^{\mathsf T}x+r\) with symmetric \(Q\).
For restricted curvature, feasible directions form the subspace \(\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inertia of \(Q\), or of its restriction to \(\ker A\), completely determines quadratic curvature.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2q^{\mathsf T}x+r\) with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), the Hessian is \(2Q\). Thus \(f\) is convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) exactly when \(Q\succeq0\), strictly convex exactly when \(Q\succ0\), and concave exactly when \(Q\preceq0\). Both positive and negative eigenvalues in the relevant matrix diagnose indefinite curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eigenvalue signs of the quadratic matrix, restricted to feasible directions when necessary, determine convexity, concavity, or indefiniteness.
