children.title: Numerical Formulation Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Numerical instability in quadratic forms, cones, derivatives, or bound-dependent formulations.

children.title: Scaling Failures
children.top_down_role: Instability caused by incompatible magnitudes in nonlinear models.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute residual tests can conceal order-one normalized violations in poorly scaled constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an absolute feasibility tolerance \(\tau>0\). For the equality \(\alpha x=\alpha\), where \(0<\alpha\le\tau\), the point \(\widehat x=0\) satisfies the unscaled residual test \[|\alpha\widehat x-\alpha|=\alpha\le\tau.\] Yet division by the natural row scale \(\alpha\) gives the equivalent equation \(x=1\), whose residual at \(\widehat x\) equals \(1\). Thus an absolute residual rule that is not invariant under positive row scaling can accept an order-one violation of an equivalent formulation. Scaling failure is avoided only when tolerances are defined relative to explicit row and variable scales, or residuals are tested in a scale-invariant norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tiny row multiplier can make an order-one violation pass an absolute residual test, although the normalized equivalent constraint clearly fails.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau>0\) is an absolute, unscaled feasibility tolerance.
\(0<\alpha\le\tau\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat x=0\) passes the unscaled test but has normalized residual \(1\).
review_flags: Concrete scaling counterexample is not supported by a supplied numerical-analysis locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly illustrates non-invariance under row scaling, but no source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Conditioning Failures
children.top_down_role: Instability caused by ill-conditioned quadratic forms, cones, or derivative systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small residuals need not imply small solution errors for ill-conditioned constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_\delta=\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta)\), \(b_\delta=(1,\delta)^{\mathsf T}\), and \(0<\delta\le\tau\), where \(\tau\) is an absolute residual tolerance. The exact solution of \(A_\delta x=b_\delta\) is \(x^*=(1,1)^{\mathsf T}\), but \(\widehat x=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}\) satisfies \[\|A_\delta\widehat x-b_\delta\|_\infty=\delta\le\tau,\qquad \|\widehat x-x^*\|_\infty=1.\] Since \(\kappa_\infty(A_\delta)=1/\delta\), vanishing residuals coexist with order-one point errors as conditioning deteriorates. Residual-only acceptance therefore cannot certify accurate primal variables without conditioning-aware backward or forward error analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ill-conditioned linear subsystem can have a tolerance-small residual while its computed point remains order-one away from the exact solution.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\delta\le\tau<1\).
Residuals are tested in the infinity norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|A_\delta\widehat x-b_\delta\|_\infty\le\tau\) does not imply a small \(\|\widehat x-x^*\|_\infty\).
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically covers conditioning-aware residual validation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual-versus-forward-error example is correct and appropriately classified, but it lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Big-M Failures
children.top_down_role: Weakness or numerical unreliability caused by bound-dependent large constants.

knowledge_statements.title: Big-M Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oversized big-M constants weaken relaxations and can interact unsafely with integrality tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min\{z:x=1,\ 0\le x\le Mz,\ z\in\{0,1\}\},\qquad M\ge1.\] Its integer optimum is \(1\), while the continuous relaxation admits \((x,z)=(1,1/M)\) with value \(1/M\); hence the root relaxation gap approaches \(1\) as \(M\to\infty\). Moreover, if an integrality test treats \(z\) as zero whenever \(|z|\le\tau_I\), then \(M\ge1/\tau_I\) makes the relaxed value \(z=1/M\) numerically indistinguishable from zero while \(x=1\). Thus excessive \(M\) simultaneously destroys bound strength and can invalidate implication semantics under finite tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As big-M grows, the relaxation bound collapses and a fractional indicator may fall inside integrality tolerance while permitting a nonzero activated variable.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation replaces \(z\in\{0,1\}\) by \(0\le z\le1\).
The numerical integrality tolerance is \(\tau_I>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxed optimum is \(1/M\), and \(M\ge1/\tau_I\) permits \(z=1/M\) to pass a zero-integrality test.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the combined relaxation-gap and integrality-tolerance failure.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The big-M relaxation and tolerance example is mathematically coherent, but the combined failure claim has no cited support.

children.title: Unsupported Globality Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Unsupported global conclusions caused by curvature errors or local nonlinear solutions.

children.title: False-Convexity Failures
children.top_down_role: Invalid global claims caused by incorrect curvature classification.

knowledge_statements.title: False-Convexity Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Misclassifying indefinite quadratic curvature invalidates convex global-optimality conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a quadratic function \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) on a convex set with nonempty interior, convexity requires the symmetric part \((Q+Q^{\mathsf T})/2\) to be positive semidefinite. If this condition is assumed but not verified, local conditions cannot support convex globality. For example, with \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), \(c=0\), and \(x\in[-1,1]^2\), the point \(x=0\) is stationary and has value \(0\), whereas \(q(0,1)=-1/2\). Any global certificate derived solely from the false declaration that this model is convex is therefore unsupported.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indefinite quadratic declared convex may have stationary points worse than feasible alternatives, so convex optimality logic yields no valid global certificate.
assumptions_latex: The quadratic domain is convex and has nonempty interior.
Globality is inferred using convex first-order logic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \((Q+Q^{\mathsf T})/2\not\succeq0\), a convexity-based global certificate is invalid.
review_flags: The supplied locators do not specifically document the quadratic curvature criterion and failure example.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The curvature criterion and indefinite-quadratic example fit the failure leaf, but no supporting source is cited.

children.title: Local-Solver Globality Failures
children.top_down_role: Unsupported global conclusions drawn from locally optimal nonlinear solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Solver Globality Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local optimality or stationarity does not certify global optimality for nonconvex continuous subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_\delta(x)=(x^2-1)^2+\delta x\) on \([-2,2]\), with \(0<\delta<8/(3\sqrt3)\). Its derivative \(f_\delta'(x)=4x^3-4x+\delta\) has three distinct roots: two are strict local minima separated by a local maximum. The positive local minimum is not globally optimal because, for every \(x>0\), \[f_\delta(-x)=f_\delta(x)-2\delta x<f_\delta(x).\] Consequently, a local nonlinear solver may return a point satisfying second-order local optimality conditions while a better feasible point exists. Such output supplies an incumbent, not a globality certificate, unless complemented by a valid global bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex polynomial has a strict nonglobal local minimum, showing that successful local-solver termination alone cannot establish global optimality.
assumptions_latex: The local solver certifies only local first- and second-order conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A strict local minimizer returned by a local solver need not minimize \(f_\delta\) globally.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the local-versus-global counterexample.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tilted double-well example supports the stated local-versus-global boundary, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Curvature Verification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Numerical regimes where curvature evidence is insufficient for global certification.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Verification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise or sampled Hessian checks do not establish convexity over an entire relaxation domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex and let \(f\in C^2(D)\). Convexity on \(D\) is equivalent to \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in D\), not merely at finitely many sampled points. For example, \(f(x)=x^4-x^2\) has \(f''(1)=10>0\), but \(f''(0)=-2<0\), so a positive curvature check at \(x=1\) does not establish convexity on any interval containing \(0\) and \(1\). A curvature-based globality claim is supported only when positive semidefiniteness is proved throughout the relevant continuous relaxation domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hessian can be positive at sampled points yet negative elsewhere; global convexity requires domain-wide curvature verification.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is open and convex.
\(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite pointwise checks of \(\nabla^2f\) do not imply \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in D\).

children.title: Tolerance-Induced Certificate Gaps

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Induced Certificate Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incompatible subsystem tolerances can leave points accepted numerically but invalid under the intended mixed-integer semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the implication encoded by \(x\le Mz\), together with \(x=1\), \(z\in\{0,1\}\), an integrality tolerance \(\tau_I>0\), and a row-feasibility tolerance \(\tau_F\ge0\). The point \((x,z)=(1,1/M)\) satisfies both algebraic rows exactly. If \(1/M\le\tau_I\), the integer validator may classify \(z\) as zero although the nonlinear or linear validator accepts \(x=1\). The intended implication at the rounded value, namely \(z=0\Rightarrow x=0\), is then violated. A combined certificate therefore requires tolerance propagation ensuring that rounding, feasibility, conic, nonlinear, and bound tests certify one common perturbed problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate validators may each accept a point while their combined rounded interpretation violates the model; certificate tolerances must describe one compatible perturbation.
assumptions_latex: Integrality and row feasibility are checked independently.
The intended semantics are evaluated after integer rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(1/M\le\tau_I\), separate acceptance does not imply validity of \(z=0\Rightarrow x=0\).

children.title: Binary Quadratic Hardness

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Quadratic Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-hardness inherited through the quadratic binary representation of weighted maximum cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with nonnegative integer weights \(w_{ij}\), assign \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) to each vertex. The cut weight equals \[\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}(x_i+x_j-2x_ix_j).\] Therefore maximizing an unconstrained quadratic polynomial over \(\{0,1\}^{|V|}\) contains weighted MAX-CUT as a polynomial-size special case. The threshold decision problem asking whether the quadratic objective is at least \(K\) is NP-hard, and it belongs to NP for rationally encoded coefficients because a binary vector permits polynomial-time evaluation. Hence binary quadratic optimization is NP-complete in decision form and admits no polynomial-time exact algorithm unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard cut polynomial embeds weighted MAX-CUT into unconstrained binary quadratic optimization, making its threshold decision form NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: Graph weights and threshold \(K\) have binary rational or integer encodings.
The number of binary variables is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Binary quadratic threshold optimization is NP-complete, and exact optimization is NP-hard.

notation.meaning: Binary side assignment for vertex i.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex MIQP Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity when the number of integer variables is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider rationally encoded convex mixed-integer quadratic programs \[\min\left\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x_i\in\mathbb Z\ \text{for }i\in I\right\},\qquad Q\succeq0.\] This class is NP-hard when \(|I|\) is variable, because choosing \(Q=0\), bounding the integer variables by \(0\le x_i\le1\), and retaining linear constraints yields binary linear optimization as a special case. Convexity of the continuous objective therefore does not imply polynomial-time solvability of the mixed-integer problem. Consequently, a general exact algorithm cannot have polynomial worst-case running time in the binary input length unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex MIQP remains NP-hard because setting the quadratic matrix to zero recovers binary linear optimization; continuous convexity does not remove combinatorial hardness.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Representation Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent convex quadratic and lifted second-order-cone encodings, with complexity measured in the chosen representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb{Q}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive semidefinite and suppose an explicitly encoded factor \(L\) satisfies \(Q=L^{\mathsf T}L\). Then the epigraph constraint \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx\le t\) is equivalent to the lifted system \(\|Lx\|_2^2\le t\), or equivalently \(\|(2Lx,t-1)\|_2\le t+1\). Thus one feasible set may be represented directly by quadratic coefficients or through a conic lift. Polynomial-time and input-size claims must charge for the selected coefficients, factor, and auxiliary variables; equivalence of feasible sets alone does not imply polynomial equivalence of encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic constraint has an equivalent conic lift, but coefficient, factorization, and auxiliary-variable encodings can have different sizes and computational consequences.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\succeq0\) and \(Q=L^{\mathsf T}L\).

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-call complexity for bounded convex mixed-integer feasibility with fixed integer dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq[-R,R]^{p+q}\) be a closed convex set containing a Euclidean ball of radius \(r>0\) whenever it is nonempty, and let a strong separation oracle return, for each rational query \(z\), either membership or a rational separating inequality. For fixed integer dimension \(p\), Lenstra-type convex mixed-integer feasibility algorithms use a number of separation calls polynomial in \(q\), the oracle output length, and \(\log(R/r)\). This oracle bound does not include the internal cost of producing a separator and is not an explicit-encoding bit bound unless that cost and output length are polynomially controlled.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear-Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between oracle-call counts and bit complexity for black-box nonlinear functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each convex nonlinear function is accessible only through an oracle returning its value and a subgradient at queried rational points. knowledge_statements.title: Lenstra-Type Fixed Integer-Dimension Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flatness-based feasibility algorithm for rational polyhedra in fixed integer dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a rational polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^p:Ax\le b\}\) with fixed \(p\). Apply an affine rounding transformation to a bounded full-dimensional section of \(P\), compute a short lattice direction \(d\in\mathbb Z^p\setminus\{0\}\), and bound the integer width \(\max_{x\in P}d^{\mathsf T}x-\min_{x\in P}d^{\mathsf T}x\). If the width exceeds the fixed-dimensional flatness threshold, recover an integer point; otherwise branch over the finitely many integral hyperplanes \(d^{\mathsf T}x=k\), reduce dimension, and recurse. Output an integer feasible point or certify \(P\cap\mathbb Z^p=\varnothing\). For fixed \(p\), the running time is polynomial in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lenstra’s method rounds the body, finds a thin lattice direction, branches over finitely many lattice hyperplanes, and runs polynomially for fixed dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(A,b\) are rational and binary encoded.
The integer dimension \(p\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a point in \(P\cap\mathbb Z^p\) or certifies emptiness in polynomial time for fixed \(p\).

children.title: Submodular Binary Quadratic Models

knowledge_statements.title: Submodular Binary Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-cut representation of pairwise submodular binary quadratic objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=c+\sum_i a_i x_i+\sum_{i<j}b_{ij}x_ix_j\) for \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). The pairwise function is submodular exactly when \(b_{ij}\le0\) for every pair. Using \(x_ix_j=(x_i+x_j-|x_i-x_j|)/2\), each pair term becomes unary contributions plus an edge-disagreement term of weight \(-b_{ij}/2\ge0\). After shifting unary terms by a constant and representing them with source and sink arcs, \(f(x)\) equals a constant plus the capacity of an associated \(s\)-\(t\) cut. Hence a minimum cut yields a global minimizer in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary quadratic objective is graph-cut representable when every pair coefficient is nonpositive; one minimum cut then finds a global minimizer.

assumptions_latex: \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), and \(l,u\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(l_i\le u_i\) for every \(i\).
Each \(f_i\) is represented exactly on \([l_i,u_i]\cap\mathbb Z\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linearly constrained integer models with coordinatewise discrete-convex costs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), and \(l,u\in\mathbb Z^n\) satisfy \(l_i\le u_i\) for every \(i\). A linearly constrained separable convex integer model has the form \(\min\{\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i):Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), where \(f_i:[l_i,u_i]\cap\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R\) is discrete convex for each \(i\). Equivalently, with \(\Delta f_i(k)=f_i(k+1)-f_i(k)\), the sequence \(\Delta f_i(k)\) is nondecreasing for \(k=l_i,\ldots,u_i-1\). Separability confines nonlinear interaction to the linear constraints; particular augmentation, proximity, or dynamic-programming complexity results require additional assumptions on \(A\), the bounds, and the representation of the functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linearly constrained separable convex integer model minimizes a sum of univariate discrete-convex costs over bounded integer vectors satisfying integral linear equations; discrete convexity means that each cost's forward differences are nondecreasing.

children.title: Bounded-Treewidth Interaction Models
children.top_down_role: Quadratic or factorable models whose interaction graphs support structured elimination.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Treewidth Interaction Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural condition on the primal interaction graph of a factorable mixed-integer model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the variables be indexed by a finite set \(V\), and let every objective or constraint factor have a scope \(S\subseteq V\). The primal interaction graph \(G=(V,E)\) has \(\{i,j\}\in E\) whenever distinct variables \(i,j\) occur together in some scope. The model has interaction treewidth at most \(\tau\) if there exists a tree \(T\) with bags \((B_t)_{t\in T}\) such that every vertex and edge of \(G\) is covered, the bags containing each vertex form a connected subtree, and \(\max_{t\in T}|B_t|-1\leq\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factorable model has bounded interaction treewidth when its variable-interaction graph admits a tree decomposition whose bags have uniformly bounded size.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) and the collection of factor scopes are finite.
Each factor depends only on the variables in its declared scope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\leq\tau\).

notation.meaning: Bag indexed by a node of the decomposition tree.

review_flags: A source explicitly connecting factorable mixed-integer models, primal graphs, and treewidth is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically precise and fits the bounded-treewidth leaf, but no locator supports its use for factorable mixed-integer interaction models.

children.title: Monotone Integer Nonlinear Models
children.top_down_role: Monotonicity-based convexification and discrete polyblock interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Integer Nonlinear Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-monotone maximization over a normal integer feasible region inside a bounded box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(u\in\mathbb{Z}_+^n\) and use the componentwise order on \([0,u]\). A set \(G\subseteq[0,u]\) is normal if \(x\in G\) and \(0\leq y\leq x\) imply \(y\in G\). A monotone integer nonlinear model is \(\max\{f(x):x\in G\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\}\), where \(f:[0,u]\to\mathbb{R}\) is componentwise nondecreasing. A polyblock outer approximation is any finite union \(P=\bigcup_{v\in V}[0,v]\) satisfying \(G\subseteq P\subseteq[0,u]\); its integer vertices provide a finite order-based relaxation interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model maximizes a coordinatewise nondecreasing function over integer points of a downward-closed set, which can be outer-approximated by finitely generated polyblocks.
assumptions_latex: \(u\in\mathbb{Z}_+^n\).
\(G\subseteq[0,u]\) is nonempty and normal.
\(f\) is componentwise nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{x\in G\cap\mathbb{Z}^n}f(x)\leq\max_{x\in P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n}f(x)\) for every polyblock outer approximation \(P\supseteq G\).

notation.meaning: Componentwise order interval from zero to v.

review_flags: A monotone-optimization source supporting the normal-set and polyblock formulation is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normal-set formulation and outer-bound inequality are plausible, but a source is needed for the exact monotone-integer/polyblock interface; “integer vertices” is also not defined when the generators are nonintegral.

children.title: Loose Relaxation Bounds
children.top_down_role: Weak lower bounds caused by loose envelopes or big-M formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Loose Relaxation Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative criterion for a weak lower bound in minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(v=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\) and a relaxation \(R\supseteq F\) with bound \(L=\inf_{x\in R}f(x)\). Validity gives \(L\leq v\). For a prescribed additive tolerance \(\delta>0\), the bound is \(\delta\)-loose when \(v-L\geq\delta\). If \(0<L\leq v<\infty\), it is \(\rho\)-loose in the multiplicative sense when \(v/L\geq\rho>1\). A family has arbitrarily loose bounds if its additive gaps or, where defined, its multiplicative ratios are unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation bound is loose when its distance or ratio from the true minimization value exceeds a stated threshold; a family is arbitrarily loose when that measure diverges.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq R\).
The displayed infima are well-defined in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\leq v\), with looseness measured by \(v-L\) or \(v/L\).

children.title: Large Integrality Gaps
children.top_down_role: Bound degradation attributable primarily to discrete relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Large Integrality Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-variable family with an unbounded multiplicative continuous-relaxation gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each integer \(M\geq2\), consider \(v_M=\min\{x:Mx\geq1,\ x\in\{0,1\}\}\). Its unique feasible integer value is \(x=1\), hence \(v_M=1\). Replacing \(x\in\{0,1\}\) by \(0\leq x\leq1\) gives \(L_M=1/M\). Consequently the multiplicative integrality gap is \(v_M/L_M=M\), which diverges with \(M\). Thus even a bounded binary linear subclass of mixed-integer nonlinear optimization can have arbitrarily large relaxation ratios when coefficients are unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The binary model forcing Mx at least one has value one, while its continuous relaxation has value 1/M, producing an unbounded integrality-gap ratio.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(M\geq2\).
The relaxation replaces binary membership only by its interval hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_M/L_M=M\to\infty\).

children.title: Large Nonconvexity Gaps
children.top_down_role: Bound degradation attributable primarily to nonlinear convexification.

knowledge_statements.title: Large Nonconvexity Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An arbitrarily large additive gap caused by discarding a reverse-convex constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(M>0\), consider the continuous nonconvex problem \(v_M=\min\{Mx:0\leq x\leq1,\ x^2\geq1\}\). Its feasible set is \(\{1\}\), so \(v_M=M\). The convex box relaxation obtained by omitting the reverse-convex inequality has value \(L_M=0\), attained at \(x=0\). Hence \(v_M-L_M=M\). The additive relaxation gap is therefore unbounded over this family, despite the variable remaining in a fixed compact interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping the reverse-convex constraint x squared at least one changes the optimum from M to zero, yielding an arbitrarily large additive gap on a fixed box.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation retains the box but omits the reverse-convex inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_M-L_M=M\to\infty\) as \(M\to\infty\).

children.title: Combined Gap Amplification
children.top_down_role: Regimes where integrality and nonconvexity weaknesses reinforce each other.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Gap Amplification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A separable family exhibiting simultaneous integrality and nonconvex-relaxation losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\geq2\) be integral and \(A,B>0\). Minimize \(Ax+By\) subject to \(Nx\geq1\), \(x\in\{0,1\}\), \(0\leq y\leq1\), and \(y^2\geq1\). The original value is \(v=A+B\). Relaxing only integrality gives \(A/N+B\); additionally dropping the reverse-convex constraint gives \(L=A/N\). Thus the combined additive gap is \(v-L=A(1-1/N)+B\), the sum of independently scalable integrality and nonconvexity losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable binary and reverse-convex model makes the total relaxation gap equal the sum of independently adjustable integrality and nonconvexity losses.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb{Z}\) with \(N\geq2\).
The combined relaxation uses \(0\leq x\leq1\) and omits \(y^2\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v-L=A(1-1/N)+B\), which is unbounded as \(A\) or \(B\) increases.

children.title: Extended-Formulation Blowup
children.top_down_role: Prohibitive formulation growth from products, disjunctions, or matrix liftings.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Formulation Blowup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension-complexity criterion for unavoidable growth of exact linear formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite mixed-integer feasible set \(F_n\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_n}\), an exact linear extended formulation is a polyhedron \(Q_n=\{(x,y):A_nx+B_ny\leq b_n\}\) whose projection onto the \(x\)-space equals \(\operatorname{conv}(F_n)\). Its size is the number of inequalities. The family exhibits extended-formulation blowup when its extension complexity \(\operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{conv}(F_n))\), the minimum such size over all auxiliary dimensions, grows superpolynomially in the encoded instance length. In this regime no polynomial-size exact linear extension exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended-formulation blowup occurs when every polyhedron projecting exactly onto the integer hull requires superpolynomially many inequalities, regardless of the number of auxiliary variables.
assumptions_latex: Each \(F_n\) is finite.
Formulation size counts linear inequalities, with equations replaceable by pairs of inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{conv}(F_n))\) is superpolynomial in the instance length.

notation.meaning: Linear polyhedron in original and auxiliary variables.
Extension complexity of a polytope P.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports extension complexity or formulation lower bounds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The extension-complexity criterion is appropriately stated as a formulation-blowup boundary, but no specific source supports the definition or superpolynomial lower-bound interpretation.

children.title: Partition Blowup
children.top_down_role: Prohibitive growth from increasingly fine domain partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition Blowup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial growth of box partitions used for piecewise nonlinear relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a \(d\)-dimensional box be partitioned by dividing coordinate \(i\) into \(m_i\geq1\) nonempty intervals and taking all Cartesian products. The resulting rectangular partition contains exactly \(K=\prod_{i=1}^d m_i\) cells. If every coordinate uses \(m\geq2\) intervals, then \(K=m^d\). Consequently, any relaxation that stores at least one distinct local constraint, estimator, or selector per cell has representation size at least \(K\), which is exponential in \(d\) for fixed \(m>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Cartesian partition with m intervals per coordinate has m-to-the-d cells, so cellwise relaxations grow exponentially with dimension when each cell needs separate data.
assumptions_latex: The partition is the full Cartesian product of the coordinate intervals.
At least one formulation item is stored for every cell.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\prod_{i=1}^d m_i\), and \(K=m^d\) when \(m_i=m\).

notation.meaning: Number of intervals on coordinate i.

children.title: Size–Strength Tradeoff Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes balancing relaxation strength against formulation or partition size.

knowledge_statements.title: Size–Strength Tradeoff Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic conditions linking relaxation accuracy to formulation growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((R_k)_{k\geq1}\) be nested minimization relaxations with \(F\subseteq R_{k+1}\subseteq R_k\), lower bounds \(L_k=\inf_{x\in R_k}f(x)\), and formulation sizes \(s_k\). For finite \(v=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), define \(g_k=v-L_k\). The sequence exhibits a size–strength tradeoff when \(g_k\downarrow0\) and \(s_k\to\infty\). A stronger, class-wide tradeoff is certified when there is a function \(S:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\), with \(S(\varepsilon)\to\infty\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), such that every relaxation in the chosen formulation class having additive gap at most \(\varepsilon\) has size at least \(S(\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation sequence has a size–strength tradeoff when its gaps vanish while its formulation sizes diverge. A stronger class-wide tradeoff gives a diverging lower bound on the size of every relaxation meeting a prescribed accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq R_{k+1}\subseteq R_k\).
\(v\) and all \(L_k\) are finite.
Formulation size and additive gap are measured consistently across the chosen class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the sequence-specific regime, \(g_k\downarrow0\) and \(s_k\to\infty\); for the class-wide regime, \(g\leq\varepsilon\) implies \(s\geq S(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: Additive relaxation gap of the kth relaxation.
Formulation size of the kth relaxation.
Class-wide size lower bound at accuracy epsilon.

children.title: Nonattainment Regimes
children.top_down_role: Lower-bounding settings where an optimal value is not attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite infimum without a minimizing feasible point on a closed unbounded set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\inf\{x:xy\geq1,\ x\geq0,\ y\geq0,\ z\in\{0,1\}\}\), where \(z\) is a dummy integer variable. Every feasible point has \(x>0\), so objective value \(0\) is unattainable. For every \(k\geq1\), however, \((x,y,z)=(1/k,k,0)\) is feasible and has value \(1/k\). Therefore the mixed-integer nonlinear problem has finite infimum \(0\) but no optimal solution. The escaping sequence shows that closed feasibility alone does not replace compact level sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed mixed-integer nonlinear set xy at least one admits objective values approaching zero along an unbounded sequence, but no feasible point attains zero.
assumptions_latex: Variables \(x,y\) are real and nonnegative.
Variable \(z\) is binary and absent from the objective and nonlinear constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf x=0\), but \(\operatorname*{argmin}x=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Positive integer indexing an escaping feasible sequence.

children.title: Unboundedness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where objective values escape without a finite bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasible-ray certificate for an objective unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem over \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), suppose there exist \(\bar x\in F\) and a nonzero direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(\bar x+td\in F\) for every \(t\geq0\) and \(f(\bar x+td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\). Then the problem is unbounded below and the ray is an unboundedness certificate. For example, \(\min\{-x:x\geq0,\ z\in\{0,1\}\}\) has the certificate \(\bar x=(0,0)\) and \(d=(1,0)\), with coordinates ordered as \((x,z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible ray along which the objective tends to negative infinity certifies unboundedness; minimizing negative x over nonnegative x supplies a mixed-integer example.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x+td\in F\) for every \(t\geq0\).
\(f(\bar x+td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in F}f(x)=-\infty\).

notation.meaning: Feasible base point of the ray.

children.title: Recession-Control Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by inadequate control of feasible recession directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Control Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of compact level-set control through escaping feasible sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v\in\mathbb{R}\), write \(F_v=\{x\in F:f(x)\leq v\}\). Recession control fails at level \(v\) if there exists a feasible sequence \((x^k)\subseteq F_v\) with \(\|x^k\|\to\infty\). If additionally \(f(x^k)\to-\infty\), the sequence certifies unboundedness below. If instead \(f(x^k)\to\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), \(\alpha=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), and no feasible point has value \(\alpha\), it certifies finite nonattainment. Thus absence of bounded lower-level sets permits both recession failure regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession control fails when a bounded-objective feasible sequence escapes to infinity; its objective limit distinguishes unboundedness from finite nonattainment.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
\(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x^k\|\to\infty\) with bounded-above objective values obstructs compact lower-level sets.

notation.meaning: Objective lower-level set at level v.
Finite limiting objective value in the nonattainment case.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lower-bound oracle is valid on \(D\) only if \(L(D)\leq \inf\{f(z):z\in F\cap D\}\), with the infimum interpreted as \(+\infty\) when \(F\cap D=\varnothing\). An infeasibility declaration is valid only if \(F\cap D=\varnothing\), and a reported feasible upper bound must be the value of a point in \(F\cap D\). An oracle reliability failure occurs if some query violates any of these implications; pruning or termination based on that answer then lacks a valid global certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle fails reliability when it overstates a lower bound, falsely declares infeasibility, or reports an upper bound without a feasible witness.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Derivative information is reliable at \(x\) only when \(\widetilde g(x)=\nabla f(x)\) or a certified error set contains \(\nabla f(x)\) and is incorporated into every deduction. Otherwise a nominal supporting cut may exclude the true epigraph. For example, for \(f(x)=x^2\) at \(x=0\), the false report \(\widetilde g(0)=2\) yields \(t\geq 2x\); the epigraph point \((x,t)=(1,1)\) violates this cut.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=[-1,1]\) and \(f(x)=-x^2\). children.title: Local Optimality Evidence
children.top_down_role: Optimality evidence confined to a continuous neighborhood.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Optimality Evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order local evidence for a mixed-integer problem obtained from a rigorously specified fixed-integer nonlinear subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the mixed-integer problem with continuous variable \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), integer variable \(y\in Y\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^p\), objective \(f(x,y)\), inequalities \(g_i(x,y)\leq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and equalities \(h_j(x,y)=0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,q\). Fix \(y=y^*\in Y\). Suppose \(x^*\) is feasible for this fixed-assignment subproblem, a constraint qualification holds at \(x^*\), and multipliers \((\lambda^*,\mu^*)\) satisfy its KKT conditions. Let \(C(x^*,y^*)\) be the associated critical cone and \(\mathcal L(x,y^*,\lambda^*,\mu^*)\) its Lagrangian. If \(d^\top\nabla_{xx}^2\mathcal L(x^*,y^*,\lambda^*,\mu^*)d>0\) for every \(0\neq d\in C(x^*,y^*)\), then \(x^*\) is a strict local minimizer of the fixed-assignment subproblem. Since distinct vectors in \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^p\) have Euclidean distance at least \(1\), this also makes \((x^*,y^*)\) a strict local minimizer of the mixed-integer problem in a sufficiently small neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KKT conditions and a second-order sufficient condition certify strict local optimality for the fixed-integer nonlinear subproblem. Integer assignments are locally isolated, so this certificate also establishes mixed-integer local optimality in a sufficiently small neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: The problem has \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(y\in Y\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^p\), twice continuously differentiable objective \(f\), inequality maps \(g_i\), and equality maps \(h_j\) with respect to \(x\).
The point \((x^*,y^*)\) is feasible, and a constraint qualification holds for the continuous subproblem obtained by fixing \(y=y^*\).
Multipliers \((\lambda^*,\mu^*)\) satisfy the fixed-assignment KKT conditions, and the Lagrangian Hessian is positive definite on every nonzero direction in \(C(x^*,y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^*,y^*)\) is a strict local minimizer of the mixed-integer problem.

notation.meaning: KKT multipliers for inequalities and equalities
Critical cone of the fixed-assignment subproblem

children.title: Fixed-Assignment Optimality Evidence
children.top_down_role: Optimality evidence conditional on a fixed discrete assignment.

assumptions_latex: The integer vector is fixed at \(y^*\).
The feasible continuous slice is \(F_{y^*}=\{x:(x,y^*)\in F\}\).
A valid lower bound \(L_{y^*}\) and feasible point \(x^*\in F_{y^*}\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality \(L_{y^*}=f(x^*,y^*)\) certifies optimality on \(F_{y^*}\) only.

notation.meaning: Feasible slice at the fixed integer assignment
Valid lower bound on the fixed slice

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lower-bound matching for one fixed integer assignment.

source_refs.locator: Using interior-point methods within an outer approximation framework for mixed integer nonlinear programming p. 225

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(L_{y^*}\leq f(x,y^*)\) for every \(x\in F_{y^*}\) and \(x^*\in F_{y^*}\) satisfies \(f(x^*,y^*)=L_{y^*}\), then \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F_{y^*}}f(x,y^*)\). The certificate consists of the feasible witness and the valid matching lower bound. It contains no comparison with feasible slices indexed by \(y\neq y^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible value matching a valid lower bound proves optimality for one fixed integer assignment, but says nothing about other assignments.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Assignment Optimality Evidence

source_witnesses.locator: Using interior-point methods within an outer approximation framework for mixed integer nonlinear programming p. 225

children.title: Globality Exclusion Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits preventing local or fixed-assignment evidence from supporting a global claim.

assumptions_latex: The variable \(y\) is binary.
Evidence is restricted to the assignment \(y=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-assignment or local optimality does not imply global mixed-integer optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary between restricted evidence and a global mixed-integer certificate.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{(y-1)^2:y\in\{0,1\}\}\). On the fixed slice \(y=0\), the only feasible point is therefore both locally optimal and globally optimal for that slice, with objective value \(1\). Nevertheless, \(y=1\) is globally feasible with objective value \(0\). Thus neither local evidence nor fixed-assignment optimality excludes a superior integer assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point can be locally and fixed-assignment optimal while another integer assignment has a strictly better objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Globality Exclusion Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 Optimality Conditions for Unconstrained Binary Quadratic Problems p. 38

children.title: Global Domain Certificate Pair
children.top_down_role: Relaxation evidence valid over the current mixed-integer domain.

children.title: Global Lower-Bound Evidence
children.top_down_role: Relaxation evidence supporting a lower bound over the current mixed-integer domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Lower-Bound Evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation-based lower-bound evidence valid over the entire mixed-integer feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq R\), let \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\phi:R\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfy \(\phi(z)\leq f(z)\) for every \(z\in F\). If a finite value \(L=\inf_{z\in R}\phi(z)\) is computed or otherwise certified, then \(L\leq f(z)\) for every \(z\in F\), and hence \(L\leq\inf_{z\in F}f(z)\). For any prescribed \(\varepsilon\geq0\), if a feasible incumbent \(\bar z\in F\) satisfies \(f(\bar z)-L\leq\varepsilon\), then \(f(\bar z)-\inf_{z\in F}f(z)\leq\varepsilon\); thus \(\bar z\) is globally \(\varepsilon\)-optimal under the absolute-gap convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation containing the feasible set and underestimating its objective supplies a global lower bound. A feasible incumbent within a prescribed absolute tolerance of that bound is globally optimal to that tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The original feasible set is \(F\), the relaxed set is \(R\), and \(F\subseteq R\).
The objectives are \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(\phi:R\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), with \(\phi(z)\leq f(z)\) for every \(z\in F\).
A finite value \(L=\inf_{z\in R}\phi(z)\) is computed or certified, and any stated optimality tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\leq\inf_{z\in F}f(z)\), and any \(\bar z\in F\) satisfying \(f(\bar z)-L\leq\varepsilon\) is globally \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.

children.title: Global Infeasibility Evidence
children.top_down_role: Relaxation or domain evidence supporting infeasibility over the current search region.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is covered by finitely many domains: \(F\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^N D_i\).
For every \(i\), a valid relaxation \(R_i\supseteq F\cap D_i\) is certified empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The collection \(\{R_i=\varnothing\}_{i=1}^N\) certifies \(F=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infeasibility certificate assembled from an exhaustive finite domain cover.

source_refs.locator: Algorithms and software for convex mixed integer nonlinear programs p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\), validity of the relaxation and \(R_i=\varnothing\) imply \(F\cap D_i=\varnothing\). If \(F\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^N D_i\), these domain certificates collectively imply \(F=\varnothing\). Without certified coverage, the same collection establishes infeasibility only on \(F\cap\bigcup_{i=1}^N D_i\), not globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Empty valid relaxations certify global infeasibility only when their associated domains cover the entire feasible search domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Infeasibility Evidence

source_witnesses.locator: Algorithms and software for convex mixed integer nonlinear programs p. 1

children.title: Certificate Validity Domains
children.top_down_role: Domain restrictions controlling where lower-bound or infeasibility evidence remains valid.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Validity Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage and aggregation conditions separating domain-restricted evidence from global lower-bound or infeasibility certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq X\) be the feasible set in the global search region, and let the finite family \(\{D_i\}_{i=1}^N\) satisfy \(X\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^N D_i\). A domain lower bound \(L_i\) is valid when \(L_i\leq f(z)\) for every \(z\in F\cap D_i\); if every domain has such a valid bound, then \(\min_{1\leq i\leq N}L_i\leq\inf_{z\in F}f(z)\). A domain infeasibility certificate is valid when it establishes \(F\cap D_i=\varnothing\); if every covering domain has such a certificate, then \(F=\varnothing\). Without certified coverage, either conclusion applies only to the covered portion of the search region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain certificates become global only with exhaustive coverage and the aggregation appropriate to their type: take the minimum of valid domain lower bounds, or certify every covering domain infeasible.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set satisfies \(F\subseteq X\), where \(X\) is the global search region.
The finite domain family is \(\{D_i\}_{i=1}^N\), with \(N\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(X\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^N D_i\).
Each claimed lower bound or infeasibility certificate is valid on its stated domain \(D_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Valid domain lower bounds yield the global bound \(\min_{1\leq i\leq N}L_i\), while valid infeasibility certificates on every covering domain yield \(F=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Lower bound valid on the ith domain

children.title: Finite-Termination Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes supporting finite exact termination of relaxation-based search.

children.title: Finite-Convergence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural settings supporting exact termination after finitely many refinements.

assumptions_latex: The algorithm maintains a finite rooted partition tree.
Processing a node either certifiably fathoms it or replaces it by its finitely many children.
Every generated node is processed after finitely many iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm terminates after finitely many node-processing iterations with its prescribed certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convergence from a finite exhaustive partition and finite node resolution.

source_refs.locator: Algorithms and software for convex mixed integer nonlinear programs p. 1
On the complexity of nonlinear mixed-integer optimization p. 533

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be the algorithm's finite rooted partition tree. Assume each processed node is either fathomed by a valid infeasibility, dominance, or optimality certificate, or expanded to its children in \(T\). If the node-selection rule processes every generated node after finitely many iterations, then after at most \(|V(T)|\) node-processing steps every leaf is fathomed or resolved. The resulting exhaustive certificates establish infeasibility or the stated global optimality tolerance, so termination is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A globally valid method terminates finitely when it can generate only a finite partition tree and resolves every generated node in finite time.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Convergence Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Algorithms and software for convex mixed integer nonlinear programs p. 1
On the complexity of nonlinear mixed-integer optimization p. 533

children.title: Finite Search-Space Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where bounded discrete or partition structure limits the search space.

assumptions_latex: The admissible integer set \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^p\) is finite.
For each \(y\in Y\), an oracle finitely returns either a globally optimal continuous-slice solution or a valid infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Enumeration terminates after exactly \(|Y|\) slice-oracle calls and returns a global solution or infeasibility certificate.

notation.meaning: Continuous feasible slice at an assignment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-call bound for exhaustive enumeration of finitely many integer assignments.

source_refs.locator: On the complexity of nonlinear mixed-integer optimization p. 533

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Query the slice oracle once for every \(y\in Y\). Discard assignments certified infeasible and retain a feasible slice optimizer of minimum objective value among the remaining assignments. Because every mixed-integer feasible point belongs to exactly one slice \(F_y\), the retained point is globally optimal; if every slice is certified infeasible, the full problem is infeasible. The procedure uses \(|Y|\) oracle calls and finite additional comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When integer assignments are finite and every continuous slice is solved globally in finite time, enumeration gives a finite global algorithm using one oracle call per assignment.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Search-Space Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: On the complexity of nonlinear mixed-integer optimization p. 533

children.title: Finite-Termination Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions under which only asymptotic progress is supported.

assumptions_latex: A global method terminates only when an incumbent and lower bound meet exactly or within a prescribed tolerance.
The relaxation sequence may improve only asymptotically, and no finite exactness or positive progress condition is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Asymptotic bound convergence alone does not guarantee finite termination.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of finite termination when bounds converge without finite exactness or sufficient progress.

source_refs.locator: On the complexity of nonlinear mixed-integer optimization p. 533

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the true optimum and incumbent value be \(U=1\), and suppose valid relaxation bounds are \(L_k=1-1/k\) for \(k\geq1\). Then \(L_k\uparrow U\), but \(L_k<U\) for every finite \(k\). Under an exact-gap stopping rule \(U-L_k=0\), termination never occurs. More generally, finite termination requires finite exactness, a positive tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) eventually reached, or another finite exhaustion argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounds may converge to the optimum forever without attaining it, so asymptotic convergence does not imply finite termination under an exact-gap rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Termination Failure Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: On the complexity of nonlinear mixed-integer optimization p. 533

children.title: Asymptotic-Convergence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Refinement regimes yielding convergence without a general finite certificate.

assumptions_latex: \(F\neq\varnothing\), \(f:F\to\mathbb R\), and \(p^*:=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\in\mathbb R\).
Each \(x_k\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_k)\to p^*\), but this convergence alone supplies no finitely checkable certificate of \(\varepsilon\)-global optimality.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinction between asymptotic value convergence and finitely checkable global-optimality evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines convergence toward the global value when the available finite-iteration evidence does not provide a general stopping certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the minimization problem \(p^*:=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), an asymptotic-convergence regime produces feasible incumbents \(x_k\in F\) such that \(f(x_k)\to p^*\). Consequently, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a finite index \(K_\varepsilon\) such that \(f(x_k)\le p^*+\varepsilon\) for all \(k\ge K_\varepsilon\). This existence statement is not by itself a finite certificate: unless the evidence available at an iteration supplies a finitely checkable global condition, such as a valid lower bound \(L_k\le p^*\) satisfying \(f(x_k)-L_k\le\varepsilon\), it need not identify or certify a qualifying iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incumbent values converge to the global optimum, so a tolerance is eventually reached, but convergence alone need not provide finite, checkable evidence identifying when global tolerance has been attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic-Convergence Regimes

children.title: Uncertified Termination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stopping based on local solutions, resource limits, or unsupported global claims.

children.title: Uncertified Heuristic Termination
children.top_down_role: Stopping based on local solutions or heuristic evidence without a global certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncertified Heuristic Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates heuristic stopping evidence from a verifiable global-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm stop at a finite index \(\tau\) and return a feasible point \(\hat x\in F\) because a heuristic predicate \(H_\tau\) holds, such as lack of recent improvement, small steps, or approximate stationarity. If the recorded evidence does not imply any valid global lower bound \(L\le p^*\) with \(f(\hat x)-L\le\varepsilon\), then termination certifies at most feasibility and the explicitly checked local or empirical properties. It does not certify \(f(\hat x)\le p^*+\varepsilon\), even when \(H_\tau\) is satisfied exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stopping for stagnation, small steps, or stationarity does not certify global optimality unless the evidence also establishes a valid global bound gap.
assumptions_latex: \(p^*:=\inf\{f(x):x\in F\}\) is finite.
\(\hat x\in F\) and \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_\tau\) alone does not imply \(f(\hat x)\le p^*+\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: valid global lower bound, when available

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinction between heuristic stopping and certified global gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and mathematical distinction between heuristic stopping evidence and a global bound-gap certificate are appropriate. However, the record contains no citation, and the inventory does not identify a section, theorem, definition, or page that specifically supports this claim.

children.title: Resource-Limited Termination
children.top_down_role: Stopping caused by time, memory, node, or evaluation limits.

assumptions_latex: \(F\neq\varnothing\), \(f:F\to\mathbb R\), and \(p^*:=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\in\mathbb R\).
Any reported \(L\) has been validated as a global lower bound, and any reported \(U\) is the value of a feasible incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Resource exhaustion alone does not imply \(U-p^*\le\varepsilon\); when a validated bound pair is available, \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) is sufficient.

notation.meaning: objective value of the best recorded feasible incumbent

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: preservation and interpretation of validated bounds at a resource cutoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the bound-based conclusions preserved when computation stops because a resource limit is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a global optimization procedure is interrupted after exhausting a time, node, iteration, or memory budget. If its best recorded feasible point is \(\hat x\in F\), set \(U:=f(\hat x)\); if it has a last validated global lower bound, denote it by \(L\le p^*\). When both quantities exist, interruption preserves \(L\le p^*\le U\), and \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) is sufficient to certify \(U-p^*\le\varepsilon\). Resource exhaustion itself adds no global-optimality evidence. If either member of this bound pair is unavailable, or if \(U-L>\varepsilon\), the pair does not certify \(\varepsilon\)-global optimality, although a separate domain-wide certificate could do so.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource cutoff preserves validated incumbent and lower bounds. Their gap certifies tolerance-global optimality when it is small enough, but exhaustion itself is not a certificate and other independent global certificates are not excluded.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Limited Termination

children.title: Unsupported Globality Claims
children.top_down_role: Global conclusions not justified by the evidence available at termination.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is an admissible model class containing instances \(I_i=(F_i,f_i)\) for \(i\in\{0,1\}\).
The point \(\hat x\) and neighborhood \(N\) are common to the compared instances, and the evidence rule depends only on feasibility and information from \(N\).
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The shared evidence \(E(\hat x)\) cannot be a sound certificate of \(f_I(\hat x)\le\inf_{x\in F_I}f_I(x)+\varepsilon\) for every \(I\in\mathcal M\).

notation.meaning: instance with feasible set F_i and objective f_i
recorded feasibility and local evidence at the returned point
region on which the evidence depends

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: indistinguishability counterexample for local evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies why evidence confined to feasibility and a local region cannot support a uniform global-optimality claim over a model class containing indistinguishable counterinstances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\) be a class of minimization instances, and let \(E_I(\hat x)\) contain only feasibility and information obtained from a neighborhood \(N\) of \(\hat x\). Suppose \(I_0=(F_0,f_0)\) and \(I_1=(F_1,f_1)\) belong to \(\mathcal M\), satisfy \(\hat x\in F_0\cap F_1\), and produce identical evidence \(E_{I_0}(\hat x)=E_{I_1}(\hat x)\). If \(I_1\) has a point \(y\in F_1\setminus N\) satisfying \(f_1(y)<f_1(\hat x)-\varepsilon\), then the shared evidence cannot be a sound certificate of \(\varepsilon\)-global optimality for every instance in \(\mathcal M\). Supporting a globality claim therefore requires additional domain-wide evidence that rules out such an indistinguishable counterinstance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two admissible instances produce the same local evidence but one has a point outside the inspected region that improves the returned value by more than the tolerance, that evidence cannot soundly certify global optimality across the model class.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Globality Claims
